blocks.text: Colophon on the Correction of the Diamond Sutra

inline.s: Since ancient times those who have explained this sutra number no less than a hundred. Of those holding peculiar views we need not speak. Among those who grasped the right purport, the three treatises of Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, and Guṇamati, together with the three commentaries of Sengzhao, Zhiyi, and Jizang, stand foremost. Thereafter the treatises of masters such as Zongli, Hanshan, Ouyi, and Xufa each contain their own essential insights, yet on the whole they do not go much beyond the ancient commentaries. Still, none has been so extraordinary and profound as the Diamond Sutra commentary of the aged lay Buddhist Jiang Weinong. His commentary expounds the meaning of prajñā both in detail and exhaustively, and moreover comprehends the other great Mahāyāna sutras as well. In the contemplation methods by which he guides students, he illumines not only the upward path of Chan but also the single mind of the Pure Land school, and more besides. Where his dharma eye is especially keen, revealing what earlier men never revealed, is this: while the Tiantai school judged this sutra to be both shared and distinct, and also perfect, and the Huayan school assigned it to the initial teaching, the layman alone judged it to be the teaching of utmost perfection and utmost suddenness. …As for his reliance on ancient editions, his examination and correction of variant characters, and his establishing of a definitive text, he is truly a devoted servant of this sutra for more than a thousand years. …Once these lectures circulate, I know that readers who open this volume will be reading not less than a hundred other sutras. The sutra says that all buddhas and the enlightenment dharmas of all buddhas issue from this sutra. Is this not made all the more luminously clear? Having finished the collation, I composed this preface out of admiration.

The Lectures on the Diamond Sutra is a posthumous work of the lay Buddhist Jiang Weinong. During the layman's lifetime the manuscript could not be brought to completion, troubled as he was from time to time by the demon of illness. After his death, through various obstacles, it came near to being lost. Can it be that this supreme and most profound secret was not to be lightly divulged, or that living beings, their blessings thin, were unable to receive and fathom the great Dharma? Otherwise, why should demonic obstructions have piled up one upon another to such a degree? I had been on intimate terms with the layman for more than twenty years, and knew that he had recited the Diamond Sutra all his life and had gained a unique understanding of it. In the summer of the jiaxu year I asked him to expound its general meaning. I recorded what I could recall and brought it home. The layman sighed and said: “The bamboo is empty-hearted; that is my teacher. Your courtesy name is Zhu, ‘Bamboo,’ and you are empty-hearted to this degree; you may be called true to your name. Rather than speak briefly for you, I would rather speak to you in full.” When the members of the Shengxin Lotus Society heard of this, they asked that it be made public. So the seat was moved to the society and the teaching was formally expounded, fixed at twice a week. Each evening he ascended the seat, and the listeners were usually several tens. I took notes on the spot, and the next day copied them out and presented them to the layman for correction. After some months the layman found the correcting too laborious and said it would be better to write it himself. So the day before each lecture he would compose several thousand characters for me to copy out. Though I continued to take notes, I had no leisure to put them in order. This dharma assembly began in the seventh month of the jiaxu year and was completed in the ninth month of the yihai year. The accumulated manuscripts filled a foot. The layman thought they still needed polishing, and that the portions missing from the first section had to be supplied, before the book could be finished. Because the layman was at home and many came to ask about the Way, his fellows planned a separate quiet room in which to support him, so that he might devote himself wholly to writing. Mr. Li Tuolian, hearing of this plan, vowed to bear the expenses alone; and so in western Shanghai three rooms were rented — the right for a bedroom, the middle for a buddha hall, the left for a lecture room — to house the layman. It was hoped that within a year the commentary would be supplemented and completed. Yet each year in the yellow plum season the layman invariably fell ill, and the illness would last for months. When he recovered, he pitied the dead and suffering of the north and south, and established Great Compassion assemblies, devoutly to release them. So it dragged on, and in the end the manuscript was not freed from draft. When I met him I would occasionally ask about it, but the layman seemed unwilling to be urged. I understood his meaning and did not ask again. In the early summer of the wuyin year the layman fell ill once more, his stomach unable to take food. Every two or three days I went to inquire after him, and seeing his illness heavier than in former years, I was deeply anxious. In the fifth month of that year he passed away in quiescence. The family came to arrange the funeral, and amid the confusion the place of this manuscript was nearly lost. I urgently sent people to search everywhere until it was found, and brought it back to examine. All were loose sheets, and here and there the order was disordered. My fellows, knowing that I had notes, pressed me to complete it. But I was busy with affairs, and from the time the layman began writing the commentary himself I had had no leisure to make a fair copy of my notes; the hasty writing of those days, viewed long after, was more than half illegible. And while the layman lived, my notes still awaited his correction before they could be free of error. To presume now to continue his work with them would also be unwise. Posthumous works of ancient worthies, incomplete and fragmentary, have often been put to press; how much more so a book already six or seven parts finished. Yet to print it, it had to be compiled and assembled, and I had no spare hours in the day, so it was set aside for several months more. Fortunately the layman's disciple Mr. Zhou Qingyuan took up the task in his heart, and so the whole manuscript was handed to him. He searched leaf by leaf and inserted the sutra text as he went. But Qingyuan too, having vowed before the Buddha to bear the suffering of beings in their place, was constantly ailing and could not avoid interruptions. When the transcription was half done, through an unexpected turn it again came near to failing at the last step. Only in the winter of the jimao year was the whole book transcribed. Such were the demonic obstructions; that it was completed in the end may be called fortunate. One day I happened to meet Mr. Li Tuolian on the road, and learned that he had come to Shanghai from Hong Kong and would soon leave. I told him of this manuscript, now ready for the press. Mr. Li was delighted and said to me: “Let the printing costs be mine to bear. If others wish to rejoice with me, I would not monopolize the merit.” And leaving funds with the Shengxin Lotus Society, he departed. Just then the lay Buddhist Fan Gunong, taking refuge in Shanghai, was lodging at the society; his consent was sought, and he took charge of the collation. Thus the book was printed in the sixth month of this year. As for its contents, profound and subtle, revealing what earlier men never revealed, pointing out at every turn where students may apply their effort in earnest — all is the speech of one who has passed this way. Readers will know it when they open the volume; there is no need to say more. I have only recounted the twists and turns of how this book came to be. This is the preface.
Written in the sixth month of the twenty-ninth year of the Republic of China by Jiang Weiqiao, dharma name Xianjue, at Yinshi Studio.

The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra is one scroll of the six hundred scrolls of the great Prajñā collection. Its words are few but its meaning is fine; that it is likened to the hardness within gold is well warranted. The six hundred scrolls of text are vast and boundless, and readers find them difficult. This one scroll is recited by every household and known to every mouth, and so the profound meaning of prajñā has been widely transmitted. Since ancient times those who have explained this sutra number no less than a hundred. Of those holding peculiar views we need not speak. Among those who grasped the right purport, the three treatises of Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, and Guṇamati, together with the three commentaries of Sengzhao, Zhiyi, and Jizang, stand foremost. Thereafter the treatises of masters such as Zongli, Hanshan, Ouyi, and Xufa each contain their own essential insights, yet on the whole they do not go much beyond the ancient commentaries. Still, none has been so extraordinary and profound as the Diamond Sutra commentary of the aged lay Buddhist Jiang Weinong. His commentary expounds the meaning of prajñā both in detail and exhaustively, and moreover comprehends the other great Mahāyāna sutras as well. In the contemplation methods by which he guides students, he illumines not only the upward path of Chan but also the single mind of the Pure Land school, and more besides. Where his dharma eye is especially keen, revealing what earlier men never revealed, is this: while the Tiantai school judged this sutra to be both shared and distinct, and also perfect, and the Huayan school assigned it to the initial teaching, the layman alone judged it to be the teaching of utmost perfection and utmost suddenness. In this he surely does not contradict what the sutra calls the Tathāgata's teaching for those of the supreme vehicle. As for such phrases in the sutra as “Tathāgata,” “Buddha,” “World-Honored One,” “Not so,” and “the Buddha told Subhūti” — things ordinary men overlook — the layman was always able to bring out their supreme meaning. Recently the Shengxin Lotus Society printed this commentary, and I assisted in its collation; I was able to read the text, and could not keep from rejoicing and leaping for joy, marvelling at what had never been. As for his reliance on ancient editions, his examination and correction of variant characters, and his establishing of a definitive text, he is truly a devoted servant of this sutra for more than a thousand years. Formerly, reading the lay Buddhist Huang Hanzhi's vernacular explanation of the Amitābha Sutra, I once sighed and said: “One who reads this explanation will know not only the meaning of the Amitābha Sutra but also the dharma of all sutras.” Now I say the same of the lay Buddhist Jiang's Diamond Sutra commentary. Once these lectures circulate, I know that readers who open this volume will be reading not less than a hundred other sutras. The sutra says that all buddhas and the enlightenment dharmas of all buddhas issue from this sutra. Is this not made all the more luminously clear? Having finished the collation, I composed this preface out of admiration.
Reverently prefaced in the early summer of the gengchen year, the twenty-ninth year of the Republic of China, by Fan Gunong.

1. This book is a posthumous work of the layman Jiang, published for the world. In the first edition, because the manuscript was unfinished, the notes of the layman Jiang Xianjue, which the layman Jiang had himself corrected at the time, were used to supply the gaps. In the second edition of the thirty-first year of the Republic of China, the missing lectures were carefully collated by the layman Jiang Xianjue from his old notes and inserted accordingly, and so the work became complete. 2. This book is divided into the four great divisions of faith, understanding, practice, and realization, and the volumes are divided accordingly. The fivefold profound meaning forms the first volume; the rest is divided into four volumes, five in all, with the layman's collation record and colophon appended at the end of the volume. 3. The outline of the divisions is placed at the head of the book, so that readers may conveniently consult it. 4. In the first edition, the compilation was undertaken by the layman Zhou Qingyuan, the collation by the layman Fan Gunong, and the proofreading jointly by the layman Jiang Xianjue and the layman Meng Dingchang. 5. Where passages are supplied in the book, the character bu, “supplement,” is added at the head of the line to keep the entries clear.
Explaining the Sutra's Title
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra
Before expounding this sutra, one must first set out its divisions. The great divisions are two.
(A) First, a general explanation of the title. Next, a separate interpretation of the text's meaning.
(A) First, again two parts: (B) First, explaining the sutra's title; next, explaining the title concerning the person.

(B) First, again three parts: (C) First, expounding the essentials of prajñā; next, clarifying the merging of the various schools; third, following the fivefold profound meaning in explaining the title.
(C) First, expounding the essentials of prajñā.
Expounding the Essentials of Prajñā

The essentials of prajñā contain three meanings. (1) It means that prajñā is the essential outline of the Mahāyāna Buddha-dharma. This meaning is found everywhere in the great Mahāyāna sutras and treatises and in the writings of ancient worthies. Were one to cite them widely, volumes would not exhaust them. Here I set aside the abundant and take the concise, in order to make it clear, and because it is easier to understand. Now the Mahāyāna teaching is deep and vast as the sea. Yet it is wholly grounded in saving oneself and saving others. For saving oneself and saving others there are countless dharma-gates. Yet they are wholly grounded in the six pāramitās. And of giving, precepts, patience, effort, and meditative concentration, the five pāramitās, if they are apart from prajñā, are not pāramitās. So these six pāramitās are wholly grounded in prajñāpāramitā. That prajñā is the essential outline of the Mahāyāna Buddha-dharma is then manifestly clear. Therefore the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra says: “Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the buddhas. The buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher. The Dharma is prajñāpāramitā.” The Great Prajñā Sutra says: “Mahāprajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas; it can give birth to the buddhas and embraces the bodhisattvas.” From this one may see that what is called the Mahāyāna, the supreme vehicle, is nothing but prajñā alone. Apart from prajñā there is no Buddha-dharma. One should know that all the teachings of the lesser and greater vehicles issue from prajñā. Among all teachings there are occasionally some resembling the highest theories of non-Buddhist schools such as the Confucians and Daoists. Prajñā alone only the Buddha can realize; only the Buddha can teach. The highest theories of non-Buddhist schools, once they meet prajñā, vanish like ice and fire. Therefore at the Huayan assembly the great bodhisattvas praised him, saying: In the heavens above and under heaven none equals the Buddha; in the worlds of the ten directions there is none to compare. All that is in the world I have fully seen; there is nothing at all equal to the Buddha. Knowing this, how can the theory that the three teachings share one source deserve even to be called absurd? Knowing this, one knows that students of Buddhism who do not thoroughly understand prajñā, though they know all the teachings and learn all the dharma-gates, are abandoning the root to chase the branches, seeking among twigs and leaves. How could they reach the other shore? Now prajñā is nothing other than the right wisdom inherent in the principle-body. The principle-body is reality-prajñā. The right wisdom is contemplation-prajñā. Both are called prajñā to show that outside principle there is no wisdom and outside wisdom no principle; principle and wisdom are one suchness. Since one is learning Buddhism, one should first open the Buddha's knowledge and vision. What is the Buddha's knowledge and vision? It is prajñā. Yet from of old few have studied it. Some are frightened at the sight of it; some speak of it ignorantly and wildly. This is why, though many study Buddhism, few realize the Way. Is this not to betray the Buddha's grace, and moreover to betray one's own spirit? Why say so? When our World-Honored One attained the Way, he marvelled, saying: “How strange, how strange! All living beings on earth possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature. But because of deluded thoughts they cannot realize it. Were there no deluded thoughts and attachments, then the wisdom without a teacher and the natural wisdom would immediately appear before them.” The Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature is reality-prajñā. Deluded thoughts are the discriminating mind, the sixth consciousness. Attachment is the view of self, the seventh consciousness. And contemplation-prajñā is what transforms these two consciousnesses. When these two consciousnesses are transformed, the storehouse consciousness and the first five consciousnesses are all transformed as well. Therefore it is said: were there no deluded thoughts and attachments, the wisdom without a teacher and the natural wisdom would immediately appear before one. These two wisdoms are precisely the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature. Because they do not come from outside and cannot be given to another, they are called “without a teacher.” Because they are inherent to the dharma-nature and must be self-awakened and self-realized, they are called “natural.” They may also be matched with fundamental wisdom and subsequently attained wisdom, or spoken of as the wisdom of the paths and the wisdom of all modes. In sum, ordinary beings are ordinary beings because of beginningless ignorance. Ignorance means, as it were, no wisdom. Therefore to transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, one need only open this right wisdom. People in Buddhist circles have a constant saying: “Seek to open wisdom.” These words rightly mean that one should open the right wisdom of prajñā — that is, open the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Our World-Honored One appeared in the world for one great matter. What is the great matter? It is to open the Buddha's knowledge and vision for all living beings, to reveal the Buddha's knowledge and vision to them, and to enable them to awaken to and enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Yet living beings, though they know to seek the opening of wisdom, do not understand why it is so. Teachers and students alike seek branches and pick leaves, never thinking to inquire at the gate of prajñā. Some even warn one another not to speak of it. What pitiable matter could exceed this? What betrayal of the Buddha's intent could exceed this? What misleading of the Dharma and of people could exceed this? From now on, I deeply wish, together with all good friends in the Dharma, to make the right meaning shine and to spread it with all our strength.

(2) What is called the essentials of prajñā means clarifying the essentials with respect to prajñā itself. As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra quoted above says, the Buddha-dharma is prajñā. It is clear that the one gate of prajñā embraces meaning without limit. If its essentials are not understood, one is liable to drift without return. Earlier men had those who took the emptiness of the supreme meaning as their thesis, those who took the two truths as their thesis, and those who took the eight negations as their thesis. Their theories differ greatly. The supreme meaning is the original nature. The nature is the absolute body, hence it is called the supreme meaning. The substance of the nature is empty and quiescent, hence it is called the emptiness of the supreme meaning. This meaning clarifies that the essentials of prajñā lie in breaking self and removing attachment. One must let go of both self and dharmas, until emotional attachment is utterly empty. As it is said, one attains the state of having nothing further to detach from, and so removes all illusions. Only then does reality appear. The two truths are the conventional truth and the ultimate truth. “Conventional” means worldly; “ultimate” means real. “Truth” carries the sense of precise and valid. The appearances of things in the world, which the common view takes as precise and valid, are called the conventional truth. The nature and principle of the real, which the sage's wisdom alone knows to be precise and valid, is called the ultimate truth. Speaking in terms of the Buddha-dharma, whatever clarifies the meaning that all dharmas arise from conditions is the conventional truth. Why? Because worldly people, not yet awakened to the original nature, follow appearances and turn with them; so one tells them that all dharmas are merely conditionally arisen, that the existent is not existent, and the meaning is settled. Whatever clarifies the meaning that conditional arising is itself emptiness is the ultimate truth. Why? Because with the sage's wisdom one sees the real nature in the midst of illusory appearances. Thus it is perfectly clear that all dharmas are not existent yet existent, and in their very substance are all empty, and the meaning is settled. The bodhisattva Nāgārjuna said: “For the sake of the worldly truth, one speaks of living beings. For the sake of the supreme meaning truth, one speaks of living beings as nonexistent.” The worldly truth is the conventional truth; the supreme meaning truth is the ultimate truth. From this we know that the conventional truth clarifies the existent that is empty, and the ultimate truth clarifies the emptiness that is existent. He also said: “The buddhas, relying on the two truths, expound the Dharma for living beings.” Therefore Master Jizang said: The Buddha-dharma does not go beyond the two truths, and the two truths comprise all Buddha-dharma. Now prajñā originally comprises all Buddha-dharma entirely. And since it is said that the Buddha expounds the Dharma relying on the two truths, it is clear that the essentials of prajñā do not go beyond the two truths. The cardinal purport of prajñā is to keep one from abiding in either emptiness or existence, so as to accord with the supreme meaning of the middle way. The two truths, real and conventional, precisely clarify this meaning.

The eight negations are: neither arising nor ceasing, neither annihilated nor permanent, neither coming nor going, neither one nor different. Through the depth or shallowness of one's delusion regarding the eight negations, the six realms come about. Through the depth or shallowness of one's awakening to the eight negations, the three vehicles come about. All living beings calculate and cling to the marks of arising and ceasing, annihilation and permanence, oneness and difference, coming and going, and so abide in existence; hence they are called deluded. Those in the three vehicles, though they do not cling to the marks of arising and ceasing and so forth, still cling to non-arising and non-ceasing and so forth, and so lean toward emptiness. Therefore the Buddha taught the meaning of the eight negations, precisely to make plain the two truths. When the two truths are clear, the middle way appears. And the meaning of the emptiness of the supreme meaning likewise causes both emptiness and existence to be emptied, so that afterward one clings to nothing, and the middle way is perfectly clear. From this we see that the emptiness of the supreme meaning, the two truths, and the eight negations, though their formulations differ, are alike in revealing the middle way. The essentials of prajñā are then nothing other than this: with respect to the two extremes of emptiness and existence, to sweep away emotional clinging and attachment, striving to exhaust it utterly, so as to reveal the perfectly fused middle way. In other words, the Buddha taught prajñā in order to enable all living beings who are caught in deluded thoughts and attachments to open the right wisdom inherent in the principle-body, to make clear their ignorance, to awaken their unawakened state, so that the reality that is neither marked nor unmarked, the Tathāgatagarbha that is neither empty nor non-empty, may appear before them, and they may together realize the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature. This is precisely the great matter for which our original teacher appeared in the world. Thus the prajñā dharma-gate is the supreme vehicle, enabling all living beings to ride it straight to the ground of buddhahood. In this light, rather than citing meanings one by one to clarify its essentials, it would be better to say: the Diamond Prajñā Sutra is in truth the essential outline of the prajñā division — and this is the more succinct way to put it. Why? Because this sutra omits no dharma and reveals no meaning incompletely; the two truths, the eight negations, and the emptiness of the supreme meaning cited above are each and all complete within it. For example: “no mark of self, no mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas” is the meaning of the emptiness of the supreme meaning. To ferry all living beings to extinction is the conventional truth. That in truth no living being is ferried to extinction is the ultimate truth. To practice giving is the conventional truth. To abide in nothing with respect to dharmas is the ultimate truth. And so with “one should not grasp dharmas, one should not grasp non-dharmas,” “is not, is called,” and the rest. Everything said throughout the sutra is nowhere other than a clarification of the meaning of the two truths. As for causing bodhisattvas to penetrate self and dharmas, it lies in opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision. What is said afterward is all the meaning of neither one nor different, neither annihilated nor permanent, neither coming nor going, neither defiled nor pure, and so on, revealing the empty mark of all dharmas and the equality of all dharmas. Now the empty mark of all dharmas and the equality of all dharmas is precisely what is called not grasping at marks, and being thus without disturbance. And it causes students thus to expound and thus to receive and hold it. Is this not to take such meanings as the essentials of prajñā? Nor is that all. As the Great Prajñā Sutra and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra quoted above say: “Prajñā can give birth to the buddhas and embraces the bodhisattvas; the Buddha-dharma is prajñā.” This points out that the essential purport of the Buddha-dharma does not go beyond prajñā. And this sutra says: “All buddhas, and the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi dharmas of all buddhas, all issue from this sutra.” Its pointing out of the essentials of prajñā lies wholly in this sutra — is this not even more luminously clear? The Buddha taught prajñā in sixteen assemblies in all, rich in meaning and abundant in text. It is said that the Tibetan translation runs to a thousand scrolls. The Chinese, being concise, still has six hundred scrolls. Among the Buddhist scriptures the prajñā division has the greatest bulk. Reading and reciting it is already difficult, let alone expounding and upholding it. Therefore in the ninth assembly, proceeding from the broad to the concise, he spoke this sutra in particular. Master Kumārajīva and his disciples translated it into Chinese, and counting also the several lines added from the Wei translation, it comes to only five thousand eight hundred and thirty-seven characters. Not only are the essential points of prajñā all contained here; having this one scroll, one holds all Buddha-dharma in one's grasp. Why? Because this scroll is the essential outline of prajñā, and prajñā is the essential outline of all Buddha-dharma. Therefore one must understand all Buddha-dharma before this sutra can be understood. Why? Because only when there is a net does one get the main cord. Yet equally, only when the purport of this sutra is deeply understood does all Buddha-dharma become clear at every point. Why? Because when the main cord is lifted, the mesh opens. This is how one should understand it. This one scroll, being the main cord of the three baskets, its importance is plain. The profundity of its meaning and the density of its order are likewise plain from this. Moreover, with few words it embraces many meanings; fortunately the translator's brush was fine enough to transmit it. Therefore every phrase and every character in the sutra bears on the great purport. Even a single name, a single word by which the compilers set it forth, contains essential meaning. With the least neglect, the meaning becomes hard to grasp. After its translation and transmission, the fifth and sixth patriarchs of Chan spread it with all their strength. Thus it became known to every household and every mouth, and circulated without cease. Though many did not understand its meaning, among students of Buddhism there were none who did not read this sutra. Among the various Buddhist countries no parallel is seen. From this alone one may see that the living beings of our land are deeply sheltered by the Buddha, which is truly cause for rejoicing. Why? Because as long as this sutra circulates without cease, the buddha-seed is unbroken. From now on, one should give special attention to how it is to be expounded and how it is to be received and held. Only thus can one repay in some small measure the Buddha's grace, and the grace of those who translated and circulated this sutra. Bearing the Tathāgata's burden, one shall attain bodhi. May I be encouraged together with all of you.

(3) What is called clarifying the essentials with respect to the Diamond Prajñā itself. The essentials of this sutra are nothing other than this: the removal of deluded thoughts and attachments. The Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature is possessed by every living being, inherent in each, lacking in none. But it is obstructed by deluded thoughts and attachments, and so cannot be realized. The Buddha appeared in the world for one great matter: for this matter. All Buddha-dharma is nothing but the dharma-gates for breaking attachment and removing obstruction. And what this sutra teaches is especially direct and to the point. It is like a diamond sword: practicing in accordance with it, one may cut through on the spot. Deluded thoughts are the discriminating mind. Attachment is of two kinds: clinging to the five aggregates and the physical body as self is called the attachment to a person, or in brief, self-attachment. Clinging to all dharmas is called the attachment to dharmas, or in brief, dharma-attachment. If self-attachment is not removed, the affliction obstruction arises. If dharma-attachment is not removed, the obstruction of the knowable arises. Together these are called the obstruction of delusion. From delusion one creates karma, which is the karma obstruction. Because of karma one suffers, which is called the suffering obstruction, also called the retribution obstruction. The two attachments, to self and to dharmas, may be further divided into the discriminate and the innate. To arouse the mind in discrimination and thereby cling is the discriminate attachment to self and dharmas; hence it is coarse. To cling with the ordinary affections, without any deliberate discrimination, as thought after thought arises together — this is the innate attachment to self and dharmas; hence it is subtle. This is the seed of habitual tendency from many lives, stored in the field of the eighth consciousness, and so it arises with every thought; it is the hardest to remove. One should know that deluded thoughts and attachments arise from beginningless ignorance. Prajñā, by contrast, is the right wisdom of the principle-body. When wisdom opens, ignorance becomes clear. When ignorance is clear, deluded thoughts and attachments are cut off of themselves. Therefore a student of Buddhism should first open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision. The Buddha's knowledge and vision is precisely the right wisdom of prajñā. Whatever dharma-gate one practices, one must devote effort to this. Hence no dharma can be apart from prajñā. It is the same with the Pure Land practice of reciting the Buddha's name. The sutra says: when the mind is pure, the land is pure. If deluded thoughts and attachments are not removed, how can the mind become pure? The ancients said: where affection is not heavy, one is not born in the Sahā world. Emotional attachment and the view of self are truly the root of affection. Therefore one who seeks birth in the Pure Land must begin here. As for what is called reciting the Buddha's name honestly, the two words “honestly” must be attended to. The world's defiling conditions and restless grasping never cease — how can one be honest? From this we know that prajñā and the Pure Land are from the first not two matters. This sutra is truly the great outline by which all students escape delusion, the pivot of the purified mind. Here I speak only briefly of the main purport; the details are in (C) three, explaining the title according to the fivefold profound meaning. The ancients, when explaining a sutra, first spoke of the profound meaning, also called profound discourse. “Profound” means deep, and also suspended: to draw out the deep meaning of the sutra, grasping the essentials and hooking the mysterious, and speak of it first, so that hearers may grasp the main points and have a thread to follow when they come to the text. Thus profound discourse is, as it were, a summary of the essentials. It is precisely where the essentials of a sutra lie. Now, following the Tiantai precedent, I open it into five layers and explain them. Thus ends the first exposition of the essentials of prajñā.
(C) Next, clarifying the merging of the various schools.

Among books explaining Buddhist sutras, there is none that has commentaries in every school and all of them still extant as this sutra. There is the hymn of the bodhisattva Maitreya, and the treatises of the three bodhisattvas Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, and Guṇadatta. But their translations are obscure and hard to read, and each expounds what he himself saw. Often a passage, at first glance contrary to the sutra's meaning, in fact completes it. Their subtle excellence later worthies could not reach. One must receive it from the great and deep places. If one dies beneath the phrases and clings to the words, matching them one by one against the sutra text, one only adds obstruction. Guifeng's Essay on the Essential Points of the Treatise and Commentary commits this fault. The very title of Guṇadatta's treatise is excellent: “The Diamond That Breaks Grasping and Attachment, Not Destroying Conventional Names.” The essential purport of the whole sutra is contained therein. The earliest of our land to annotate this sutra was Sengzhao, an intimate disciple of Kumārajīva. He wrote little ink, only briefly explaining one or two essential points. Yet it is an unalterable work. Of the annotations of the Six Dynasties still extant today, there are the commentaries of the two masters Jizang of the Three Treatises school and Zhiyi of the Tiantai school. Jizang's life energy lay in the three treatises; every work he wrote was fine. But his Commentary on the Meaning of the Diamond Sutra was a work of inattention, perhaps recorded at random by his disciples and never revised. For it has much idle text and a tangled brush; it is quite unlike Jizang's other works. Zhiyi's exposition follows Sengzhao's annotation throughout, only occasionally adding a word or two of clarification. Zhiyi used the three truths to expound every sutra; for this sutra alone he took the two truths as his thesis. And in the phrase “is called” he everywhere took it as a conventional name. The patriarch's dharma eye commands our admiration. It is hard to understand why the descendants of the Tiantai house did not follow the patriarch's instruction. Could they not have seen this book? (Zhiyi's commentary was only retrieved from Japan by the lay Buddhist Yang Renshan at the end of the Qing and printed.) In the Tang, Kuiji of the Dharma Characteristics school also wrote an annotation, much of it expounding dharmas and marks. There is also the annotation of Shi Huijing, whose subtlety is not inferior to Sengzhao. Among ancient annotations, those of Sengzhao and Huijing are the best. Guifeng of the Huayan school wrote an Essay on the Essential Points of the Treatise and Commentary. Though carefully composed, unfortunately it is bound to the treatise's text, and the sutra's meaning is obscured instead. In the Song there was Master Changshui, who wrote a Record of Definitive Collation to explain Guifeng's Essay. It follows the text and explains the meaning, and is very detailed. Chan patriarchs also wrote works expounding the sutra, such as the sixth patriarch in the Tang, Zhongfeng in the Yuan, and Hanshan in the Ming. Yet all are brief pieces with little development. At the end of the Ming, Ouyi of the Tiantai school wrote the Treatise on the Diamond Breaking Emptiness. It was written with a purpose, and may serve as one style among others. Besides these, in the Song, Ming, and Qing, among those who left home and those who remained at home, explanations of this sutra are found everywhere. There is not wanting here and there a phrase that hits the mark, but precision and soundness they did not achieve. In the early Qing there was the Tiantai master Puwan's Commentary on the Seal of the Mind, which expounds the sutra by the three truths. Its words are often too literal and greatly contrary to the sutra's purport, yet its divisions here and there have something to recommend them. There is also the Huayan master Datian's Commentary on the New Eye, which here and there is penetrating and can reveal what earlier men never revealed. His division of the sutra by faith, understanding, practice, and realization shows a particularly lofty standpoint. As for the rest, such as the Annotations of Fifty-Three Houses, they are mixed and impure and not worth regarding. In this present exposition of the sutra, the emphasis is on carving out one by one the profound and subtle purports of the sutra. Where earlier men took it as the initial gate of the Mahāyāna, I speak of each point's ultimate meaning and bring it home to perfect fusion. Where earlier men paid no attention, I open up its great purport. Where earlier men called a phrase repetitive, I distinguish its depth and shallowness. At every point where the meanings before and after are linked and hooked together, I state one by one why it is so, and thread them through. In all the gates of contemplation and gates of practice, wherever the work of cultivation is pointed out, I dare not neglect a single character. My aim is that hearers may find a place to begin. I cite many other sutras to corroborate one another, so that they may find where they converge. In the essential places, I moreover bring them home to the Pure Land, to break the long-standing fault of discrimination against it. I am ashamed that my learning is shallow and insufficient to expound this profound sutra. Yet where my great vow lies is truly the wish that everyone may clearly understand the true meaning of prajñā, so that they need not fear to speak of it, speak of it wildly, or speak of it shallowly. As for the essential sayings in the treatises and commentaries of former worthies cited above, I have selected them one by one and taken them in. I need not follow their outward appearance or be bound by their words. Thus ends the next, clarifying the merging of the various schools.
The Fivefold Profound Meaning
(C) Third, explaining the title according to the fivefold profound meaning.
Two parts: (D) First, a general explanation of the divisions; next, explaining them in order.
(D) First, a general explanation of the divisions.

The five layers are name, substance, thesis, function, and aspect. “According to” means that Master Zhiyi of the Tiantai school, expounding the title of the Lotus Sutra, opened it into five layers — name, substance, thesis, function, and aspect — in order to bring out the essential purport of the sutra, which is the clearest and most concise way. One layer fewer will not do; one layer more is also unnecessary. Therefore I follow it here. These five layers give rise to one another in order. Now a sutra must have a name that stands uniquely for it. The name is what marks out a sutra's essential purport, showing how it differs from other sutras. Therefore the first layer is explaining the name. The name is the guest of the reality. Once the name is marked out, there must be a reality behind it; it is not set up in vain. Therefore next the substance is revealed. The substance is the real substance, the principal body of the sutra's name. For the name has been checked against reality. Yet without cultivating contemplation and practice, it remains an empty name. And to cultivate in reliance on the substance, one must clarify the thesis and purport. Therefore third, the thesis is clarified. The thesis is the thesis of practice, the purport of cultivation. Once there is true cultivation, one must obtain its function. Therefore fourth, the function is discussed. “Function” means efficacy. The Buddha, according to the capacities of living beings, great or small, sharp or dull, taught various dharmas to teach and transform them. Therefore the sutra teachings differ as lesser or greater, partial or perfect, gradual or sudden. For example, the Huayan school judges them as the five kinds of teaching — lesser, initial, final, sudden, and perfect; the Tiantai school judges them as the four methods of conversion — the tripiṭaka, shared, distinct, and perfect, and the four manners of conversion — sudden, gradual, secret, and indeterminate. Once the name, substance, thesis, and function of a sutra, the four layers of profound meaning, are clear, then which kind of teaching it belongs to may also be understood. Therefore the fifth layer is judging the aspect of the teaching. Now, following the order of the five layers, I open them into five sections.

(D) Next, explaining them in order, in five parts: (E) First, explaining the name; next, revealing the substance; third, clarifying the thesis; fourth, discussing the function; fifth, judging the aspect of the teaching. (E) First, again two parts: (F) First, the common name; next, the specific name.
(F) First, the common name.

The common name is the word “sutra” in the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra. What the Buddha taught is commonly called sutra; it is not so for this sutra alone. Therefore the word “sutra” is the common name of all Buddha-dharma. In Sanskrit it is sūtra, also written as sūtra in other transcriptions. The original meaning of sūtra is a thread, extended to mean threading through, embracing and holding, and according with. When the dharmas taught by the Buddha were classified, gathered, and made into books, they were accordingly named sūtra. It means threading through the Buddha's words, embracing and holding them without loss, according above with the Buddha's mind and below with the capacities of living beings. When the great Dharma came east, the ancients accordingly translated sūtra with the character jing. The original meaning of jing is warp and woof, weaving and organizing, which exactly corresponds to sūtra's senses of thread, threading through, embracing, and holding. Moreover, by our country's custom, only the words of sages may be called jing, which is extremely solemn. To translate sūtra as jing is most apt. But our character jing does not contain the sense of according with, so compared with sūtra's original meaning it falls somewhat short. Yet apart from jing there is no other character by which to translate it. Therefore the ancients, at a loss, called Buddhist books “accordant sutras,” both to supply the original meaning and to show that these are Buddhist sutras, not the sutras of other teachings. As for explaining jing as “constant” or as “the Way,” this is an extended meaning of the character jing; sūtra originally had no such meaning. Therefore in explaining Buddhist sutras it should not be cited.
(F) Next, the specific name.

The seven characters of Diamond Prajñāpāramitā are the name set uniquely for this sutra; they cannot be used in common for all sutras, and so are called the specific name. “Diamond” is the simile; “prajñāpāramitā” is the dharma. This is establishing the name by dharma and simile. In the titles of sutras, the ways of setting a name take no more than seven senses, namely person, dharma, simile, single, compound, and complete. For example, the Amitābha Sutra: Amitābha is a buddha's name; taking a person's name as the sutra's title is called establishing the name by person alone. The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sutra: pratyutpanna-samādhi is a kind of dharma-gate; this is establishing the name by dharma alone. The Rice Stalk Sutra: the rice stalk is a simile for dharmas arising from conditions; this is establishing the name by simile alone. The Lotus Sutra: “Wondrous Dharma” is the dharma, “Lotus” is the simile; having both dharma and simile, it is neither single nor compound, and is called establishing the name by dharma and simile. The Chapter of Samantabhadra's Vows: having both dharma and person, this is called establishing the name by person and dharma. The Tathāgata's Lion's Roar Sutra: the Tathāgata is the person, the lion's roar is the simile; this is called establishing the name by person and simile. The Great Expansive Buddha's Flower Adornment Sutra: “Great Expansive” is the dharma, “Buddha” is the person, “Flower Adornment” is the simile; this is establishing the name with person, dharma, and simile all complete. The single are three, the compound three, the complete one, seven in all. If in one title there are two similes and no person or dharma, it is still single simile and not compound. Where there are two dharmas or two persons, by this example it may be known. Therefore though sutra names are without limit, the senses taken are only these seven.

In Sanskrit, vajra means diamond; it is the name of a substance. It is the essence of gold, hardest and sharpest. It can destroy all things, which is its sharpness. No thing can destroy it, which is its hardness. The Buddhist scriptures say that Indra has a treasure called the vajra; holding it, he does battle with the asuras. The weapon held by the vajra warriors is called the vajra club. The golden-wheel king has a vajra-wheel treasure, and so is called the golden-wheel king. It was originally a celestial treasure. Though it also exists in the human world, it is very rarely seen. The ancients called it adamantine spar, its color like amethyst, transparent. Some say it grows on stones at the bottom of the water. In the scriptures it is often used as a simile for dharma and for persons, as in vajra-samādhi, vajra warrior, vajra body, vajra net, vajra hand, vajra mind, and so on. All take the sense that it is firm and indestructible, and can destroy all demonic obstructions. Here it is used as a simile for the right wisdom of prajñā. Prajñā is like a great mass of fire: it cannot be touched from any side; touch it, and one loses body and life. Like the diamond, no thing can touch its edge. The right wisdom of prajñā can shatter the heavy obstruction of affliction, as the diamond can destroy all things. Master Kumārajīva said: the diamond treasure is an inch square, and its light can illumine several tens of li. The light of prajñā-wisdom is likewise: it penetrates and sees all ordinary affections and deluded thoughts, and shatters ignorance. The diamond treasure only a vajra warrior can hold. So too with prajñā: one who does not possess the capacity of the Mahāyāna cannot bear it. Therefore it is said: one who delights in the lesser dharma, clinging to the views of self, person, living being, and life span, cannot hear, receive, read, and recite this sutra, or explain it to others. The Tripiṭaka master Paramārtha said the diamond treasure has various colors. The blue one can dispel calamity: like prajñāpāramitā, which can remove the three obstructions, accomplish the three bodies, cross the stream of birth and death, reach the shore of nirvāṇa, and ferry all suffering and distress. The yellow one grants whatever is sought: like prajñā's adorning of the ten thousand practices and its accomplishing of boundless merit. The red one emits fire toward the sun: like prajñā's using initial enlightenment to join original enlightenment, sending forth the fire of wisdom to burn the firewood of affliction, like a thousand suns whose light shines everywhere. The white one clarifies muddy water: like prajñā's turning the back on dust and joining with enlightenment, crossing the five turbid ages and reaching the pool of coolness. The green one subdues poison and harm: like prajñā's removal of the attachments to self and dharmas and its dispelling of the suffering of the three poisons. There is also a colorless diamond, also called the empty-colored one; one who obtains it can walk and stand in empty space. So too with prajñā: the so-called emptiness of the supreme meaning. With the wisdom of these three emptinesses, self is empty, dharmas are empty, and emptiness itself is empty. In emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formation, or consciousness, and even no wisdom and no attainment, and yet one attains supreme bodhi. Still it comes down to no dharma whatever being attainable. Then one is thus without disturbance, and accomplishes the vajra body. In sum, the diamond's hardness is a simile for reality-prajñā, which is unchanging though it follows conditions, and undestroyed though wrapped in defilement. The diamond's sharpness is a simile for contemplation-prajñā, which breaks through every self and cuts off every delusion. The diamond's brightness is a simile for textual prajñā, which can open the wisdom of understanding and make ignorance clear. The diamond is a supreme treasure whose value cannot be measured, a simile for prajñā as the supreme dharma-treasure whose merit cannot be measured. The diamond treasure is rarely seen in the world, a simile for the rarity of the prajñā dharma-treasure: the so-called supreme, most profound, and subtle dharma, hard to encounter in a hundred thousand million kalpas.

In Sanskrit, prajñā means wisdom. It is not worldly knowledge or petty cleverness. It is the right wisdom inherent in the principle-body, what is called the Buddha's knowledge and vision. The principle-body is the awakened nature, also called reality-prajñā. Right wisdom is contemplation-prajñā. Outside principle there is no wisdom, outside wisdom no principle; principle and wisdom are from the first one suchness, and so both are called prajñā. Because it was feared that people would mistake it for ordinary cleverness, the sutras and treatises mostly use the transliterated sound prajñā. This wisdom is inherent in all living beings, but is obstructed by beginningless ignorance and cannot appear. Moreover, this wisdom is known only by self-verification; it cannot be described by words and letters. Why? Because only when words are cut off and the activity of mind is extinguished can one verify it for oneself. Yet all living beings have been blind to it for so long. Without skillful means, how shall the cloud of obstruction open? And if the obstruction does not open, how can this wisdom appear? Therefore our World-Honored One appeared in the world for this great matter. Having no other way, he still used words and letters to guide them. Whatever speaks of the Buddha's knowledge and vision to reveal it to living beings so that they may awaken and enter — this is called the prajñā dharma-gate, also called textual prajñā. It is meant to enable living beings, by means of words, to arouse contemplation and realize reality. All the other dharma-gates he taught, such as giving and observing precepts and the rest, issue from the Buddha's knowledge and vision, and are meant for living beings to practice in reliance on them as aids to opening the right wisdom of prajñā. Therefore it is said: no dharma is apart from prajñā, and prajñā is the essential outline of all dharmas. In other words, prajñā is the main trunk of all dharmas, dwelling within all dharmas, and not existing apart from all dharmas. In plain terms, our Buddha appeared in the world out of compassion for living beings who all possess the Tathāgata's awakened nature and can all become buddhas, yet do not know it. So he spoke of what the Buddha himself had verified, in order to break the foolishness of living beings. Set against foolishness, it is provisionally called wisdom. In truth wisdom is nothing other than awakening. Reality-prajñā is original enlightenment. Contemplation-prajñā is initial enlightenment. Because all living beings have never been awakened, textual prajñā is provisionally used to awaken them. For this reason, in reading sutras and hearing the Dharma, the essential thing is to be deeply watchful over oneself, taking what the Buddha said as a mirror, and at all times and in all places using it to reflect oneself. Without observing and reflecting, how shall delusion become awakening? This is what is meant by relying on words to arouse contemplation. When the work of contemplation has long continued, then a solemn and watchful mind arises of itself — this is initial enlightenment, and the first opening of the right wisdom inherent in the principle-body. If one does not retreat or slacken, and the work of contemplation grows daily deeper and purer, then what is called initial enlightenment becomes like the new moon, gradually with more light and less darkness, until the moon's disk is full and its radiance brilliant, and the nature-substance appears. This is initial enlightenment joining with original enlightenment, and there is no longer any division of initial and original. One should know that becoming a buddha is nothing other than the perfect clarity of the awakened nature. And the opening of the awakened nature cannot come about without relying on the power of textual prajñā. Therefore it is said that all buddhas issue from this sutra. Furthermore, in the Sanskrit text, jñāna means wisdom-knowledge and prajñā means insight-understanding. To illumine and see is jñāna; to understand and comprehend is prajñā. To decide is jñāna; to discern and choose is prajñā. To know the conventional truth is jñāna; to illumine the ultimate truth is prajñā. To penetrate the wondrous existent is jñāna; to awaken to true emptiness is prajñā. The sutras often speak of the six pāramitās, and sometimes open them into ten. The seventh is skillful means, the eighth is vow, the ninth is power, the tenth is jñāna, set against the sixth, prajñā. Yet emptiness is the emptiness that is the existent, and the existent is the existent that is emptiness. Therefore the two words wisdom and insight are in truth divided yet not divided. This sutra precisely clarifies not abiding in either emptiness or existence. Therefore the word prajñā should be understood as wisdom and insight together; one must not cling to the letter and force a division into two. It is only that sometimes in the sutras, without dividing, a division is made, citing jñāna to clarify the conventional truth and citing prajñā to clarify the ultimate truth. Therefore students must not fail to know this meaning either.

The diamond is originally used as a simile for prajñā. Yet only what was spoken in the ninth assembly is likened to the diamond's ability to cut through. Is this not because the meaning taught in this sutra is especially hard and sharp and clear, and especially able to cut off delusion? What other assemblies spoke of was gold; what this sutra speaks of is the essence within the gold. Therefore this sutra says: the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma issue from this sutra. It also says: the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is also inconceivable. Pointing precisely at this sutra, it shows that the essentials of prajñā lie wholly in this sutra, which is proof enough.

In Sanskrit, pāramitā means “arrived at the other shore.” Following our language, it should be “reaching the other shore.” Among the ancient customs of India, whatever was brought to its utmost was called “arrived at the other shore,” like our dialect's “arrived home.” Speaking in terms of the Buddha-dharma, it means leaving this shore of birth and death, crossing the midstream of affliction, and reaching the other shore of nirvāṇa. Therefore pāramitā is also a metaphorical term.

Nirvāṇa is non-arising and non-ceasing; it means the original nature. As for the original nature, “original” carries the sense of being inherent. To say it is inherent shows that it is not made. Since it is not made, one can see that it is so from the first, and not something that came to be out of nothing. Therefore it is said to be non-arising from the first. To say it was already present from the first shows it is not newly produced. Since it was not arising from the first, it now also does not cease. That living beings' birth and death continue without end is the mark, not the nature. Why do birth and death continue without end? Because their mind arises and ceases without pause. One should know that the mind whose arising and ceasing never pauses, what is called the mark of consciousness, is also not the nature. Why is it so? Because of affliction. Through affliction the mind comes to have arising and ceasing, and the nature turns into consciousness. From this one creates karma and receives the suffering of transmigration. Living beings do not know to return to the source, but take consciousness as the nature and are deluded by the marks of birth and death; hence transmigration never rests. And so, though face to face with the non-arising and non-ceasing, they are forever separated from it. Therefore affliction is likened to the midstream, birth and death to this shore, and nirvāṇa to the other shore. Originally there is no this shore and other shore; because the midstream separates them, the division of here and there comes about.

Affliction is also called delusion, namely the delusions of view and thought. The delusions of view and thought all arise from the view of self. Therefore to be freed from the marks of birth and death, one must realize the non-arising and non-ceasing nature. And to realize the original nature, one must transform and remove the view of self. Yet the view of self is deep-rooted, and one must use various methods to tame it and open fundamental wisdom to cut it off. As it is said: though the principle is suddenly awakened, the matter must be removed gradually. It is like crossing over: going from this shore to the other shore, one proceeds gradually and cannot hurry. Therefore it is called leaving, crossing, and reaching, to show that it cannot be arrived at in a single step. And the word “stream” is used again to show the danger: the wind of ignorance must never rise, for if it rises one follows the current downward, and may even meet the calamity of drowning — how then could one cross to the other shore? Let practitioners be careful. Yet what has been said above is still spoken solely with respect to ordinary beings. If one distinguishes more finely, birth and death contain two layers, and affliction also includes the delusions of view and thought, of dust and sand, and of ignorance. Ordinary beings abide in existence and cling to a person and a self; hence through the delusions of view and thought they fall into fragmentary birth and death. The two vehicles and one class of bodhisattvas abide in emptiness and cling to dharmas and a self; hence through the delusions of dust and sand and of ignorance they have transformation birth and death. Therefore to realize nirvāṇa without residue, one must empty both emptiness and existence, break the two attachments to self and dharmas, and end the two layers of birth and death. Crossing the midstream of the delusions of view and thought, dust and sand, and ignorance, one then reaches the other shore of nirvāṇa. Therefore the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra says: “The two views of existence and nonexistence both belong to this shore. Only when the two attachments are both empty does one reach the other shore.” The two attachments are the attachments to self and to dharmas. What is the raft for crossing the stream? The six pāramitās. By these six methods one can reach the other shore. Therefore these six are also called the six crossings. Among the six, giving is essential, and prajñā is especially essential. Giving is letting go. If one does not know how to let go, how can one be willing to leave this and cross over? Yet without the wisdom of contemplation, how can one be willing to let go? Therefore prajñā is the essential outline of the five pāramitās. Apart from it, the five are not pāramitās. Furthermore, the two words wisdom and insight, spoken separately, may also be called insight at the causal stage and wisdom at the fruition stage. Prajñāpāramitā, spoken of the causal stage, means the contemplative insight that reaches the other shore. Spoken of the fruition stage, prajñā itself is pāramitā. Why? Because at the fruition stage prajñā is principle and wisdom as one suchness. Principle and wisdom as one suchness is non-arising and non-ceasing. Spoken of the causal stage, the diamond is a simile for this contemplative insight, hardest, sharpest, and brightest, and so able to reach the other shore. Spoken of the fruition stage, the diamond is a simile for the Tathāgata's dharma body, the so-called vajra indestructible body. Thus ends the explanation of the name.
Revealing the Substance
(E) Next, revealing the substance, in three parts: (F) First, clarifying the meaning of substance; next, distinguishing sameness and difference; third, directly revealing the substance.
(F) First, clarifying the meaning of substance.

Substance means the principal body. Whenever one expounds a sutra, it cannot be finished in a few words; often there are thousands of words and a tangle of threads. Readers and hearers, like people entering the great sea, see only a vast expanse and cannot tell the ford or the shore, and cannot help sighing at the ocean's immensity. One should know that every sutra, however great its bulk and however numerous its divisions, must have a place where it comes home. In other words, every sutra must have its own principal point. Thousands of words all press toward this point; thousands of threads all arise from this point. This point is the principal point of the sutra, what is called the substance. To seek out the one principal point amid thousands of words and thousands of threads, and to point it out — this is called revealing the substance. If readers and hearers understand the principal point of the sutra, then the essential outline is in their grasp, and they will not sigh at the ocean, nor count sand in the sea, nor stray onto wrong roads. Knowing this, one knows how very important the revealing of the substance and the rest really is. Knowing this, one knows the painstaking care with which the ancients spoke of profound discourse before the sutra. In sum, what is called substance here is the substance of the sutra, not the substance of the nature.
(F) Next, distinguishing sameness and difference.

Distinguishing sameness and difference has two senses. First, with respect to the sutra's substance and the nature's substance, their sameness and difference are distinguished. The sutra's substance is not the nature's substance; that is settled. Yet the Buddha appeared in the world for one great matter. What is called the one great matter is precisely to open and reveal to all living beings that they alike possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature, so that they may awaken and enter it and all become buddhas. He taught the Dharma for forty-nine years solely for this matter. In this light, no sutra is other than the revealing of the inherent buddha-nature. Thus the principal body of every sutra is nothing but the unfolding of the nature's substance, as is clear. Then why did the text above say that what is revealed here is the sutra's substance and not the nature's substance, as if a distinction had to be drawn? One should know that although no sutra is other than the revealing of the inherent buddha-nature, each sutra's teaching has a different purport. Some emphasize removing obstruction; some emphasize cultivating merit; some speak of former causes; some speak of later effects. Capacities differ in thousands of ways, and so the teachings differ in thousands of ways accordingly. Not every sutra points directly at the original nature and unfolds it thoroughly. How could one be vague and muddled, and stubbornly insist that the sutra's substance is the nature's substance? And even speaking of directly pointing at the original nature: the nature's substance embraces all things, and one name cannot exhaust its measure. So, at a loss, various names were set up, such as true suchness, thusness, reality, dharma realm, dharma body, the substance of pure and luminous nature, perfect enlightenment, the mind of self-nature purity, and so on; their names are without limit and the meanings revealed are likewise without limit. Sutras that point directly at the original nature cite one of these names, or another, or several at once, according to the differing purport of the sutra. From this one can see that although they are all sutras pointing directly at the original nature, the meanings they reveal each differ, and the place where the sutra comes home likewise differs. Therefore the sutra's substance and the nature's substance — speaking of sutras that thoroughly reveal the nature — are two yet not two, and still not two yet two; they cannot be lumped together as one. This is why their sameness and difference must be clearly distinguished.

Next, with respect to the various schools, their sameness and difference are distinguished. Whatever the school, in explaining a sutra's title one must take in the essential purport of the sutra and unfold it, if one's words are to have substance. As for setting up categories and divisions with a fixed standard, the two houses of Tiantai and Huayan must be reckoned foremost. Yet Huayan's ten divisions are sometimes not very applicable, and are not so clear and to the point as the five layers established by the Tiantai house. Take the revealing of the substance: the two houses also differ considerably in their approach. The substance revealed is the same, but the intent of the revealing differs greatly. The Huayan school mostly reveals the substance from the word “sutra,” the common name — that is, it reveals the substance with respect to the teaching that does the expressing. The great masters of this school often said: all Mahāyāna sutras take all dharmas' reality as their substance. Guifeng's Essay on the Essential Points of the Diamond Sutra says: textual prajñā is the substance. Both speak with respect to the teaching that does the expressing. Now if all Mahāyāna sutras take all dharmas' reality as their substance, then all Mahāyāna sutras are plainly textual prajñā. And if one points precisely at the prajñā division, then what was spoken in all sixteen assemblies is textual prajñā. How could it be so for the ninth assembly alone, or for this sutra alone? Therefore what Guifeng says may be applied to other sutras as well. Hence it is said that he reveals the substance from the word “sutra,” the common name. The Tiantai house, however, in revealing the sutra's substance, points precisely at this one division, and it cannot be transferred. That is, it reveals the principal substance of this sutra from the seven characters of the specific name, Diamond Prajñāpāramitā — that is, it reveals the substance with respect to the principle and the phenomena that are expressed. Therefore it is said that what the Tiantai house establishes is clear and to the point. This is the sameness and difference of the two houses in revealing the substance.
(F) Third, directly revealing the substance.

Now, since we follow the Tiantai standard and use the sutra title's specific name to reveal the principal body of the meaning clarified by the sutra, we cannot but first know what the great masters of the Tiantai house have said. Of the Tiantai worthies' commentaries on this sutra that have come down to us, in which the man is worth taking as a teacher and the commentary worth transmitting, there are only two. One is Zhiyi's commentary of the Sui. One is Ouyi's Treatise on Breaking Emptiness of the Ming. Zhiyi took “if one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathāgata” as the sutra's substance. Ouyi took “reality is permanently abiding” as the sutra's substance. Recently the Tiantai master Dīxian wrote a New Commentary on the Diamond Sutra, taking “the emptiness of the supreme meaning” as the sutra's substance. The three masters' formulations differ, and one might fear confusion. Yet there is no need to doubt. One should know that the three accounts differ only in words; in principle they are no different. Reality is precisely the emptiness of the supreme meaning. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra says: “What is called the emptiness of the supreme meaning is the reality of all dharmas.” The title Tathāgata reveals the virtue of the nature, that is, it reveals the virtue of the dharma body. And the dharma body is nothing other than reality. From this one may know that the three accounts, though differing, are in fact the same. Yet the emptiness of the supreme meaning in the New Commentary is a phrase not found in this sutra. Zhiyi's commentary is best, and this sutra has an even more concise and essential phrase to offer. “Reality” is apt and essential, but the two words “permanently abiding” seem somewhat forced. If one cited only the two words “reality,” though wonderful, still every Mahāyāna sutra takes all dharmas' reality as its substance, and it would seem too vague and general. Therefore I do not insist on the three accounts, but change it to this: the sutra's substance is “giving rise to reality.” This sutra says: “When faith is pure, reality is then produced.” Reality is neither marked nor unmarked; that is, it is true suchness and the dharma body, and also the Tathāgatagarbha that is neither empty nor non-empty. “Produced” means appearing before one. How does it appear before one? Through purity of mind. How is the mind made pure? Through non-abiding. Non-abiding means being free of all marks. To be free of all marks is to abide in neither emptiness nor existence, which is to be empty through and through. This sutra says: “Free of all marks, one is then called a buddha.” Why? Because when marks are gone, reality appears before one. From this we see that using the three words “giving rise to reality” to reveal this sutra's homecoming leaves no principle uncomprehended and no matter unrevealed. This sutra itself explains the meaning of reality, saying: “Reality is precisely no-mark.” The word “no” here negates them all: not existent, not empty, not both existent and empty, not neither existent nor empty. Since all these marks — empty, existent, both, neither — are all negated, and negation too is not established, this is being free of all marks. The aspect of living beings' own nature is from the first like this, and truly like this. There is no way to name it, so it is forced to be called reality. “Free” means non-abiding. “Non-abiding” means not grasping. Not grasping at marks, one is thus without disturbance. There is no way to name it, so it is forced to be called “produced.” Textual prajñā expresses this reality. Contemplation-prajñā contemplates this reality. And as for reality-prajñā, when it appears in full, one has reached the other shore. Grasping at marks arises from the view of self; when all marks are gone, the view of self is removed and affliction is cut off. And with each portion of affliction cut off, a portion of reality is produced. The reason this sutra's textual prajñā and contemplation-prajñā are likened to a diamond is precisely that it can cut off affliction and give rise to reality. The three words “giving rise to reality” as the principal substance of the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra — is this not luminously clear?
Clarifying the Thesis
(E) Third, clarifying the thesis. Three parts: (F) First, clarifying the meaning of the thesis; next, distinguishing sameness and difference; third, directly clarifying the thesis.
(F) First, clarifying the meaning of the thesis.

What is called clarifying the thesis is clarifying practice. “Thesis” means principal. “Clarifying” means explaining. Now why is clarifying practice called clarifying the thesis? The Tiantai school sets it up in this way, and there are two layers of deep meaning: first the general, second the particular. (1) It warns and spurs students on, because the Buddha-dharma takes actual practice as principal. This is the general meaning. (2) The methods of practice are without limit, and differ according to capacity and purpose, just as in worldly schools, where according to the various categories certain subjects are set as required and others as elective. This sutra has inconceivable merit. It is spoken for those who have aroused the greater and the supreme vehicle. What method of practice is principal for it? This is the particular meaning. That it says clarifying the thesis rather than clarifying practice takes its sense from this.

Clarifying the thesis follows closely upon revealing the substance. For though the principal body of the sutra's meaning has been revealed, without practice it cannot be realized. If one knows only how to reveal the substance, and does not cultivate in reliance on the substance, one is like one who counts another's treasure, having not half a coin of his own. What benefit is the revealing? Therefore whenever our Buddha taught a dharma, before speaking he always exhorted them to listen attentively. To possess the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and practice is attentive listening. And at the close of every sutra he always said: “having believed and received it, they practiced accordingly.” This is to say that opening and revealing, reading the sutra, and hearing the Dharma take practice in accordance with the teaching as principal. Now the place where this sutra comes home, the principal body of its meaning, I know to be the giving rise to reality. But how must reality be given rise to? Our Buddha's every phrase speaks of the nature, and so every phrase speaks of practice. Now if one is to practice in accordance with the Dharma, among the countless gates of practice, which dharma does the sutra's purport take as principal? For this reason, after revealing the substance there must follow the clarifying of the thesis.

The word “thesis” in the phrase “clarifying the thesis” as said above, and the “thesis” of the various schools and factions; again the “thesis” of schools and the “thesis” of religion; again the “religion” spoken of in Buddhist circles and the “religion” spoken of in the world — not only do worldly people not understand these, but even people in Buddhist circles are much confused about them. Now I take the occasion to distinguish their points of sameness and difference one by one, which I imagine you would wish to hear. What people today call religion takes its meaning originally from the leavings of Westerners' wit. Such books exist in the world, and I have no leisure here to touch on the details. It may be put briefly thus: within a teaching, one is honored as possessing supreme authority and is taken as lord. This lord can make people live or die; all flourishing and withering lies in his hands, and so he is worshipped. This is the worldly account of religion. Therefore the single word “religion” already carries the sense of superstition and dependence. Worldly people, seeing only that in Buddhist circles the Buddha is honored as the founder, and hearing also that Buddhist circles speak of their “religion,” do not understand what it means, and so confuse it with the Western religion, turning on the heels of others, sneering at it as superstition, slandering it at will, and creating the karma of uninterrupted hell. Truly pitiable. And because Buddhist circles bow to images, they revile it as worshipping wooden puppets, meaning that Buddhism is inferior even to other teachings, than which foolishness nothing could be greater. Here there is no need to discuss the thesis deeply or cite the teachings at length; a single phrase may judge that it is utterly different from the Western religion. One should know that buddha images, sutra scrolls, and those who have left home are called the three gems that abide in the world. The intent is to cause people, by means of images, to contemplate the Buddha; by means of sutra scrolls, to penetrate the principle; and by means of those who have left home, to arouse a mind that transcends dust and leaves defilement. Hence they are called “abiding in the world.” By borrowing the three gems that abide in the world, one contemplates the three gems of one's own nature and realizes the three gems that permanently abide. Birth and death, flourishing and withering, all depend on oneself. Supreme authority is held in one's own hand. Therefore it is said: all dharmas are mind only, and outside the mind there is no dharma. This is why the Buddha-dharma surpasses all worldly morality and philosophy. How could other religions even dream of it? As for what Buddhist circles mean by “religion,” the “thesis” means clarifying the mind and seeing the nature, because the Buddha-dharma takes clarifying the mind and seeing the nature as principal. The “teaching” means all the sutras' meanings, because all the sutras' meanings are what the Buddha revealed as teaching. Therefore if one penetrates the mind and nature, it is called penetration of the thesis. If one penetrates the sutras' meanings, it is called penetration of the teaching. Thesis and teaching are two utterly distinct matters. How could honoring one of supreme authority as the master of a teaching be meant? Thus the name “religion” is the same, but the meaning is utterly different, as is luminously clear.

Therefore the “thesis” in Buddhist circles' “thesis and teaching” does not originally refer to schools. But because the Chan gate alone takes self-awakening to the mind and nature as principal and does not emphasize the sutra teachings, it is called “a separate transmission outside the teachings,” and so is called “under the thesis.” This shows that it accords with the guiding principle of taking the clarification of mind and the seeing of nature as principal. The “teaching” in “thesis and teaching” likewise does not mean the founder. One who deeply penetrates the sutras' meanings, relies on the words, arouses contemplation and practice, and realizes reality, is called “under the teaching.” This shows that one can practice in accordance with the teaching. This is a later meaning, and already contains a sense of schools. Yet the terms “under the thesis” and “under the teaching” were equal in meaning, with no ranking at first. Later, “under the thesis” came to mean not only Chan but also to imply that one can actually practice and grasp the essentials.
