And “under the teaching” came to refer generally to all schools outside the Chan gate, and to imply seeking only wide learning with no benefit to others. So the one was weighted and the other lightened, with a great difference that cannot be mentioned in the same breath. This meaning is even later, arising when Chan was at its height.

As for the so-called schools, each has what it principally holds. Some hold to dharmas and marks, such as the Ci'en school, also called the Dharma Characteristics or Consciousness-Only school. Some hold to the dharma-nature, such as the Chan school and the Three Treatises, Tiantai, and Huayan schools. And because some rely on the teachings and some do not, the Chan school is distinguished from the others that speak of the nature. The “under the thesis” and “under the teaching” spoken of above also set up school names according to the different sutra meanings they principally hold, such as the Three Treatises school, the Lotus school, the Huayan school, the Pure Land school, and the Esoteric school; those who principally hold the precepts are called the Precepts school. Distinguishing further within a school gives what is called a faction. For example, the Dharma Characteristics school has the old faction of Paramārtha and the new faction of Xuanzang. The Huayan Sutra clarifies both nature and marks, and so those who take Huayan as their school comprehend both nature and marks in their teaching. Speaking in terms of dharmas and marks, the Huayan house may also be called yet another faction of the Dharma Characteristics. Likewise the Pure Land school has the distinction of visualization and of reciting the name. The Chan school's division into the five houses of Linji, Weiyang, Caodong, Fayan, and Yunmen, though it sets up school names, is in fact the sense of factions. The rest may be inferred. In sum, the “school” of the schools, because their established meanings and their teaching differ one from another, sets up various school names. Nor is it only that their methods of practice differ. As for the “thesis” of clarifying the thesis, it speaks solely of practice. Broadly, the “thesis” of “thesis and teaching” has the widest meaning. The meaning of schools is already narrower. And “clarifying the thesis” is narrower still. This is their difference. Yet the sense of the character for thesis — as assertion, as principal purport — is the same in all. As for what Westerners call religion, it is the sense that one of supreme authority is the master of a teaching. It is utterly different from what we call “thesis and teaching.” All this must be distinguished. Worldly people who do not understand this meaning are not to be blamed. But people in Buddhist circles, because the sameness and difference have not been distinguished, do not know how to set forth clearly and in detail the right meaning of “thesis and teaching” in Buddhist circles. They merely say that the Buddha-dharma is not a religion, in order to contend with the world. Now the Buddha-dharma plainly has a thesis and a teaching — how can it be said not to be a religion? In the writings of the ancients this appears again and again. How can such a formulation win people's hearts? If the right meaning were explained, so that they knew our “thesis and teaching” is not their “religion,” then clear as the Jing and Wei rivers, they would have no way to apply their slander.

Again, the schools other than Tiantai also clarified the thesis. Yet what they clarified is not what the Tiantai school clarified. Their sameness and difference must also be distinguished. For example, the second patriarch Zhiyan of the Huayan school, annotating the Wei translation of the Diamond Sutra, said: the three prajñās of textual, contemplative, and reality are the thesis of the sutra. What is thus called the thesis is neither devoted solely to the work of practice nor pointed precisely at the Diamond Sutra; it can only be called a general discussion of the principal purport of the prajñā sutras. Guifeng's commentary takes reality-prajñā and contemplation-prajñā as neither one nor two as the thesis, which is slightly better than the former account. Yet it too is only a general discussion, not a precise pointing at this sutra. And it speaks of nature and practice together, not solely of practice. The Three Treatises school's Jizang says in his Commentary on the Meaning: cause and effect are the thesis. That is, the practice of non-abiding is the cause, and the attainment of nothing-to-attain is the effect. This account points precisely at this sutra and cannot be transferred to another division; it is much more to the point. Yet it already touches on the fourth layer of the Tiantai house, the discussion of function. Why? Because function belongs to the effect. From this we know that the various houses agree in clarifying the thesis, but the theses they clarify differ. And from this we see all the more how clear and to the point the Tiantai house's five layers are, beyond the reach of other houses.
(F) Third, directly clarifying the thesis.

What are the Tiantai worthies' accounts of clarifying the thesis? Zhiyi's commentary marks the thesis as cultivating the giving of no marks with the wisdom of reality. Prajñā is the right wisdom inherent in the principle-body, hence “the wisdom of reality.” “Giving” is dāna; it takes the sutra's meaning that the bodhisattva should practice giving with the mind abiding in nothing with respect to dharmas. Ouyi's Treatise on Breaking Emptiness takes the contemplation that accords with principle as the thesis. “According with principle” means according with the principle-body, which is the same as Zhiyi's “wisdom of reality.” Master Dīxian's New Commentary takes the arousing of the bodhi mind as the thesis. Of the three accounts, Zhiyi's is by itself the finest; the other two are somewhat broad. Here, relying on the sutra's own ready phrases — “one should be free of all marks and arouse the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi mind,” “free of all marks, one is then called a buddha,” and “with no self, no person, no living being, no life span, cultivating all good dharmas, one then attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi” — I summarize them in two phrases: being free of all marks and cultivating all good is the wondrous thesis of this sutra's cultivating in reliance on the substance. The intent is the same as Zhiyi's, but the phrasing is the sutra's own and is clear and easy to understand, so I have changed it. How is the intent the same as Zhiyi's? This sutra cites giving alone to embrace the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices. To practice giving is precisely what is called cultivating all good. And being free of all marks is precisely the wisdom of reality. For neither dharmas nor non-dharmas are grasped; this is being free of all marks. It corresponds exactly to the reality that is neither marked nor unmarked. Then is being free of all marks anything other than the wisdom of reality? One should know that this sutra has only one thesis of practice, in the two words “non-abiding.” Just marking out non-abiding to clarify the sutra's thesis, the whole sutra's gates of contemplation and gates of practice are all contained therein. Yet fearing it is not easy to grasp, it is better to clarify it with the two phrases “free of all marks” and “cultivating all good,” and then the sense of non-abiding is perfectly clear. Why say so? Non-abiding is not abiding in either extreme; that is, being empty through and through. The sutra says: one should not grasp dharmas, one should not grasp non-dharmas; non-dharmas are not non-dharmas; and the phrases “is not” and “is called.” It also says: no mark of self, no mark of dharmas, and also no mark of non-dharmas. Whether spoken of the two extremes or of repeated emptiness, all is what is called being free of all marks. That is the true explanation of non-abiding. And immediately after “with respect to dharmas one should abide in nothing” comes “practice giving,” which is the sense of cultivating all good, and also the sense that emptiness too is not abided in. Everything said in the whole sutra about the gates of contemplation and the gates of practice is wholly grounded in being free of all marks and cultivating all good. This is precisely what is called wondrous existence that is not existence, true emptiness that is not empty,concealing and illumining at once, exactly according with the supreme meaning of the middle way. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra says: “The essential purport of prajñā lies in being free of all dharmas, which is all dharmas.” Being free of all dharmas is being free of all marks. Being all dharmas is cultivating all good. Having grasped this sutra's two phrases, being free of all marks and cultivating all good, the essential purport of prajñā becomes perfectly clear and one has a place to begin. Therefore this sutra is the essential outline of prajñā. Moreover, only by being free of all marks does one arouse the supreme bodhi; and the attainment of supreme bodhi is likewise nothing but being free of all marks. Why? Because no self, person, living being, or life span precisely means being free of all marks. And being free of all marks must be carried out by cultivating all good. This is precisely the sense that the unreal comes out of the non-unreal, and non-doing comes out of doing. Therefore the two phrases being free of all marks and cultivating all good exhaust without remainder the whole journey of the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā from this shore, across the midstream, to the other shore. Hence it is called the wondrous thesis of cultivating in reliance on the substance. In sum, clarifying the thesis must correspond to revealing the substance. The sutra's substance being the giving rise to reality, and being free of all marks being originally the wisdom of reality, therefore by being free of all marks and cultivating all good, reality is given rise to accordingly. Hence it is said: free of all marks, one is then called a buddha. Hence it is said: with no self, person, living being, or life span, cultivating all good dharmas, one then attains anuttarā-bodhi. For one who is called a buddha is so because he has attained anuttarā-bodhi. Anuttarā-bodhi is reality-prajñā. Being free of all marks and cultivating all good is contemplation-prajñā. Because contemplation realizes reality, citing these two lines of the sutra to clarify the thesis of practice is like grasping the main cord of a net, with no tangle left.
(E) Fourth, distinguishing the function.

Function means efficacy, power and use — that is, what is called the result. One who practices must attain its thesis, because otherwise no result can be expected. Now that the thesis of practice is clear, what is its result like? Moreover the result is not of one kind; one must distinguish which is greatest. What is greatest? The result that corresponds to the sutra's substance. For where there is this substance, there must be this function. If the function does not accord with the substance, then one's cultivation is not yet complete, and it cannot be called a result. Therefore it says not “revealing the function” or “clarifying the function,” but necessarily “distinguishing the function,” for this reason. Nor is that all. Function issues from the thesis. The thesis of practice belongs to the cause, the function to the effect. As the cause is, so the effect afterward is. And it says “distinguishing” to distinguish whether the effect accords with the sutra's substance, that is, to distinguish whether the cause of practice accords with the sutra's substance. One should know that clarifying practice is called clarifying the thesis because it clarifies the guiding principle of the cause of practice, which must not depart from the sutra's substance. In other words, the principal method of practice takes the sutra's substance as its thesis. Then the method of practice must accord with the sutra's substance — this is clear. And cause and effect are from the first one suchness. Therefore with respect to the student, one should distinguish whether the result he obtains accords with the sutra's substance; then one may know whether his cause of practice accords with the sutra's substance. And with respect to the sutra's meaning, one should distinguish within the sutra which function corresponds to the sutra's substance, for that is the result that is one suchness with the thesis of practice. In sum, substance, thesis, and function must be one continuous thread. And the names substance, thesis, and function are spoken with respect to the object, that is, with respect to the sutra's meaning. For revealing the substance reveals where the sutra's meaning comes home, which is the sutra's principal substance. Clarifying the thesis explains the principal method of practice spoken of in the sutra, which arises in reliance on the substance. Distinguishing the function distinguishes the greatest function spoken of in the sutra, obtained through practice. If spoken with respect to the person who practices, clarifying the thesis clarifies practice at the causal stage, and distinguishing the function distinguishes realization at the fruition stage, while revealing the substance reveals the goal of cause and effect. For clarifying the thesis clarifies that at the causal stage one must practice thus in order to be walking toward the goal. Distinguishing the function distinguishes that what is called realizing the fruit must obtain such a function in order to have reached the goal. This is how one should understand it.

Other schools, on the layer of distinguishing the function, either omit it or put it another way. For example, among the Huayan ten gates there is one called the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching. The Ci'en school also speaks of what the teaching arose for. Both discuss a sutra's function. Yet their discussions are somewhat too elaborate. Speaking of the Tiantai school, Zhiyi in his commentary on this sutra takes the two words “breaking attachment” as the sutra's great function. The Treatise on Breaking Emptiness says: the sutra's function is cutting off doubt. And the New Commentary says: the sutra's function lies in non-abiding and giving rise to mind. These are again too brief, and do not exhaust the measure of the function spoken of in the sutra. One should know that the reason substance, thesis, and function must be revealed, clarified, and distinguished is chiefly to give those who hear the Dharma a direction and to provide warning and spur. It is by no means only a matter of summing up the sutra's purport in a few phrases so that one may clearly understand where the sutra's essentials lie. Above all it must be clear and easy to understand, so that it startles the eye and alarms the mind, and one has a place to begin. Too elaborate or too brief are both unsuitable. Now, to distinguish in detail this sutra's great function, one must first clarify why living beings come to be and where the root of their inability to escape suffering lies.

The Buddha said: all living beings possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature, but because they are obstructed by deluded thoughts and attachments, they cannot realize it. These few words state it with the utmost thoroughness. The meaning is that all living beings can become buddhas. Why? Because they all possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature. Yet they cannot become buddhas — why? Because something obstructs the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature that is inherent in them. This clarifies why living beings come to be. Now all living beings possess this nature and do not know it themselves. Even if they know it, if what obstructs it is not removed completely, they still cannot realize it. This clarifies why they cannot escape suffering. What is the obstructing thing? Deluded thoughts and attachments. This clarifies the root of the sickness by which living beings come to be and receive suffering. In a few short words it is all said at once. Deluded thoughts are the discriminating mind. Attachments are the two attachments to self and to dharmas, that is, what is called the view of self. Coarsely, one clings to the physical body; this is the view of a person and a self, and one cannot escape the suffering of fragmentary birth and death. Subtly, one clings to all dharmas; this is the view of dharmas and a self, and one cannot escape the suffering of transformation birth and death. Nor is that all. Because of the attachment of the view of self, the delusion of discrimination arises. Then one is greedy for what accords with oneself and angry at what opposes oneself, not knowing that there is originally no self at all; this is called delusion, also called ignorance, also called unawakened. Thus one creates all kinds of karma and is bound and dragged by it. The more one suffers, the less one can escape. Deluded thoughts and attachments therefore grow deeper and heavier, and the inherent Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature grows more deluded and more separated accordingly.

From what, then, does the view of self arise? From not penetrating the one true dharma realm. The dharma realm is the ten dharma realms of the four sages and six ordinary kinds. Though the marks of the ten dharma realms differ without limit, the nature of the ten dharma realms is the same one true suchness. Not to penetrate is not to know. Therefore the Awakening of Faith says: “Because they do not penetrate the one dharma realm, unawakened thought arises, and there is ignorance.” Because they do not penetrate it, it is called unawakened ignorance. The arising of thought means deluded thoughts and attachments. Not penetrating the one true dharma realm is another way of saying not knowing that one possesses the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature in common with all. For not knowing that the substance of the nature is fundamentally the same, one arouses the thought of discrimination between self and others. Karmic power is created from this, and suffering retribution is summoned from this. To escape suffering retribution, then, one must dissolve karmic deeds. To dissolve karmic deeds, one must remove the view of self — this is clear. It was for this that our Buddha appeared in the world for the one great matter, and for this that he taught the Dharma for forty-nine years. This sutra is the essential outline of all dharmas, likened to the diamond's ability to cut through, and its great function lies precisely here.

The sutra is named Prajñāpāramitā because it can open in living beings the wisdom that reaches the other shore, so that they may all reach the other shore together. This wisdom is inherent in the principle-body of all living beings; it is the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature that all living beings possess, and so it is called the wisdom that reaches the other shore. Therefore when this wisdom opens, one can reach the other shore. Why? Because if this wisdom opens, the unawakened become awakened and the ignorant become clear. One penetrates the one true dharma realm. One breaks the view of self at its root. Then no delusion is left uncut. Therefore it is likened to a diamond. How, then, is this wisdom opened? One should know that arousing the mind of great compassion is opening this wisdom. Why? Knowing that all living beings possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature, but have not realized it because of obstruction, one knows that the substance of living beings' nature is the same. Therefore to see living beings suffer is to suffer oneself; to see living beings rejoice is to rejoice oneself. If one living being has not realized the Tathāgata, then the substance of the nature is still impaired. Therefore one resolves in mind to uproot their suffering, to grant them happiness, and to ferry them to buddhahood. This is called the mind of great compassion, what is called the one-substance great compassion. To be able to arouse this mind is called initial enlightenment. Though called initial enlightenment, it is at once the same as perfect enlightenment. Therefore to arouse the one-substance great compassion mind is called arousing the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi mind, whose meaning is supreme, perfect, and universal enlightenment. Hence only by being free of all marks does one arouse this mind.

Being free of all marks clarifies that one converges and returns to the one true suchness nature. How is this said? Seeing that there are living beings who can become buddhas and resolving to ferry them is not grasping non-dharmas, and is also not denying living beings. That there is a supreme bodhi to be attained is being free of the mark of no-mark. And knowing again that living beings inherently possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature, so that though one ferries them, in truth nothing is ferried, and though they become buddhas, in truth nothing is accomplished — this is not grasping dharmas, and is not denying living beings. To attain supreme bodhi yet have nothing attained is being free of the mark of a mark. When the marks of existence and nonexistence are both gone, this is called converging and returning to the true suchness nature, because one accords with the reality that is neither marked nor unmarked. Then at the first arousal of the mind, the discriminating mind is already dissolved, and the coarse and subtle views of self are quietly melted away. Therefore this sutra's meaning is likened to a diamond.

Consider this sutra: as soon as it opens its mouth it causes one to arouse the supreme bodhi mind, to ferry all living beings into nirvāṇa without residue, and yet in truth no living being is ferried into extinction. Everything said afterward unfolds this meaning. It further causes one to forget that it is a bodhi mind, and points directly at the source of mind, causing one to enter where not a single thought arises. In the latter half, the chapter opens by dislodging attachment to the arousing of the bodhi mind, until it says: “self-view is not self-view, therefore it is called self-view.” Then not a trace of the view of self remains. Therefore this sutra's greatest function lies first in breaking the self.

All living beings, because they do not awaken to the fact that the ten dharma realms share one true-suchness dharma body, cling to self and other and give rise to discriminating views. Thus they produce the three poisons, create immeasurable karma, receive the suffering of karmic bondage, and fall into transmigration. The more deluded, the more they suffer; the more they suffer, the more deluded. Even if by former good roots one meets a good teacher who teaches one to arouse the mind and take refuge in the three gems, yet by former karma one's inner and outer obstructive conditions rise in layers and circle round one another, so that one cannot practice, or practicing, finds it hard to succeed. Therefore for practitioners, repentance of karmic obstruction is of the utmost importance. The great bodhisattvas at the Huayan assembly still included this gate among their conduct and vows, let alone ordinary beings. Yet karmic deeds are of two kinds: those that can be repented, and those that admit of no repentance. If the deed is extremely heavy and has become fixed karma, repentance is especially difficult. The sutra says: “Sit upright and contemplate reality; this is called true repentance. Heavy sins are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them.” This clarifies that to dissolve heavy sins one must contemplate reality, and only then is it possible; no other method can repent them. If one sees this sutra merely as causing one to contemplate emptiness, that is still a shallow account, a one-sided view. One should know that the sutra's text causes one to abide in neither emptiness nor existence, illumining both extremes at once — this is called contemplating reality. Why? Because reality is neither marked nor unmarked. If one only contemplates emptiness, one stops at contemplating no-mark without contemplating the unmarked, and how is that contemplating reality? The sutra uses the wisdom that contemplates reality as a simile for the sun, precisely because the sun travels through the sky without abiding in the sky. Therefore the Chapter of Conduct and Vows says: “Also like the sun and moon that abide not in the sky.” If one only contemplates emptiness, one abides in emptiness; how could that be the meaning of the sun as a simile? One should know that the wisdom of reality is born of great compassion. Because of great compassion, one broadly cultivates the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices and obtains immeasurable merit. Therefore the sutra's wisdom contains merit within it, and only then does it accord with contemplating reality. Cultivating both merit and wisdom, contemplating emptiness without abiding in emptiness, one is like the sun shining brilliantly, able to dispel darkness and to give birth to all things. By such contemplation and practice one can dissolve heavy sins like frost and dew. This is how one should understand it. To understand thus is right understanding. The function of this sutra is likewise. The sutra's substance is the giving rise to reality, which is reality-prajñā. Its thesis of practice is being free of all marks and cultivating all good, which is contemplation-prajñā, that is, contemplating reality. For being free of all marks is contemplating emptiness, cultivating wisdom. Cultivating all good is not abiding in emptiness, cultivating merit. Contemplating reality and cultivating both merit and wisdom is true repentance. Therefore one can dissolve heavy sins and fixed karma. Then inner and outer obstructive conditions are all melted away at once, and what practice will not succeed? As this sutra says: “This person's former-world karmic deeds should have led him to fall into the evil paths; but because in this world he is lightly despised, his former-world karmic deeds are thereby dissolved, and he shall attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.” “Evil paths” means heavy sin. “Should have led him to fall” means fixed karma. Fortunately, having good roots, in this life he has not fallen. He is able to hear this sutra and deeply understand its purport. He can know the thesis of practice and advance in merit and wisdom together. Therefore he can receive heavy sins lightly and dissolve former karma. Why? Speaking by way of antidote, merit can dissolve sin; speaking by way of the supreme meaning, wisdom can uproot karma. “He shall attain bodhi” clarifies that what he practices will surely be accomplished. For this reason this sutra has yet another great function, namely the dissolving of karmic deeds.

Those of the two vehicles can contemplate emptiness and awaken themselves, breaking the view of a person and a self, but the view of dharmas and a self remains; because their wisdom is shallow, they cannot break it completely. The ultimate result they can achieve is only arhatship and pratyekabuddhahood. Those of the greater vehicle, though they can abide in neither emptiness nor existence, and not only awaken themselves but practice the six pāramitās to awaken others, yet have not purified ignorance completely. That is, the subtle attachment to dharmas is not yet transformed and removed, because they have not obtained the diamond wisdom. Therefore they only partially realize the dharma body and have not reached the ultimate. What this sutra calls the accomplishment of the foremost and rarest is only the attainment of perfect universal enlightenment, not yet the supreme. If one can, with respect to this sutra, deeply understand its purport, have faith without opposition, and fully receive, hold, read, and recite it and explain it to others, then one bears the Tathāgata's anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. One should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rarest dharma, and even gives rise to merit and dissolves sin, and shall attain supreme bodhi. Therefore this sutra has yet another great function: it can ultimately accomplish anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Gathering the three points distinguished above, they come to eight characters: breaking the self, dissolving sin, and accomplishing the Tathāgata — this is this sutra's great function. Thus it corresponds reasonably well with the sutra's text about this sutra having inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit. The sutra says: “The mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi.” The ancients also said: “Only exhaust the ordinary affections; there is no other sage's understanding.” The mad mind and ordinary affections are the view of self of deluded thoughts and attachments. One should know that the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature is inherent in living beings, and is only obstructed by the view of self. If this obstruction is removed, the awakened nature is from the first perfectly accomplished, wisdom is freely and perfectly clear, and the Tathāgata emerges from the shell of ignorance and appears in fullness. Therefore it is said: the mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi. Only exhaust the ordinary affections; there is no other sage's understanding. Hence though the dharma-gates of practice are without limit, the one guiding principle is simply the removal of obstruction. The great function of this sutra, to speak exactly, is likewise only the removal of obstruction.

And when one speaks of obstruction, it naturally has three. What is called accomplishment may likewise be opened into three. The first is the obstruction of delusion, also called the affliction obstruction, namely the delusions of view and thought. View, extremity, perverted, attachment to view, grasping at precepts, greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt — these number ten, and all take the view of self as their root. Therefore when the self is broken, the delusion obstruction is removed, and the virtue of prajñā is accomplished. The second is the karma obstruction. This sutra says: former-world karmic deeds are thereby dissolved. Therefore when sin is dissolved, the karma obstruction is removed, and the virtue of liberation is accomplished. The third is the retribution obstruction. Retribution means the body of suffering retribution. When the Tathāgata is accomplished, the retribution obstruction is removed, and the virtue of the dharma body is accomplished. Therefore this sutra's great function is to remove the three obstructions and accomplish the three virtues. That it here cites breaking the self, dissolving sin, and accomplishing the Tathāgata is because these are easy to understand, and the meaning of removing the three obstructions and accomplishing the three virtues is contained within them.

It was said above that substance, thesis, and function are one continuous meaning. How are they one? Let me now speak of them together. Speaking with respect to the sutra's meaning that is expressed, revealing the principal body of its homecoming is the giving rise to reality. For those who arouse the greater and supreme vehicle, this shows the goal of cultivating the cause and realizing the fruit. As for the thesis of practice, being free of all marks and cultivating all good: speaking with respect to the sutra's meaning, being free of all marks is what is called no-mark, and cultivating all good is what is called the unmarked. Yet good dharmas are not good dharmas, therefore they are called good dharmas. So to speak ultimately, cultivating all good embraces the meaning of neither marked nor unmarked, while being free of all marks is the meaning that marks and the markless are both absent. This corresponds exactly with the substance of giving rise to reality. For the ultimate meaning of giving rise to reality is likewise that marks and the markless are both absent, and that arising is non-arising. Speaking with respect to the person who practices, it is not abiding in either extreme, being empty through and through, and advancing toward the ultimate goal of giving rise to reality. As for distinguishing the function — breaking the self, dissolving sin, and accomplishing the Tathāgata: speaking with respect to the sutra's meaning, breaking the self is the function obtained by being free of all marks, because delusion is exhausted and the mind is emptied. Dissolving sin is the function obtained by cultivating all good, because merit and wisdom increase. It may also be said that breaking the self and dissolving sin are the function obtained jointly by being free of marks and cultivating good, because through the work of contemplation-prajñā, when faith is pure, reality is given rise to. For when one abides in neither extreme and the mind accords with absolute purity, then one breaks one portion of ignorance and realizes one portion of the dharma body. The view of self and karmic deeds arise from ignorance. When ignorance is broken, the two obstructions of delusion and karma gradually dissolve, and one can realize the dharma body. The first realization of the dharma body is the arising of reality. As for accomplishing the Tathāgata, it is when the work of contemplation is pure and reality-prajñā appears in fullness — how could it be only like the first rising of the moon? Speaking with respect to the person who practices, this is the perfection of cause and the fullness of fruit, having reached the goal and arrived at the other shore of nirvāṇa. Thus ends the distinguishing of the function, which also supplies what was not fully said in revealing the substance and clarifying the thesis, and distinguishes substance, thesis, and function according to the object and the person, gathering them into one continuous thread and explaining their meaning.

(E) Fifth, judging the aspect of the teaching. Two parts: (F) First, a general discussion; next, the direct judgment. (F) First, again two parts: (G) First, explaining the terms; next, a general discussion of the aspects of teaching.
(G) First, explaining the terms.

The character “judging” here has two senses. One is dividing and judging, the sense of discerning. The other is appraising, the sense of determining. To judge the aspect of the teaching means to discern the purport of the sutra and determine to what category it belongs. “Teaching” means instruction, that is, the sutra itself. The Buddha taught the Dharma to instruct living beings, and the dharma he taught was gathered into books and called sutra; hence the sutra is called the teaching. The Buddha's appearing in the world to give teaching was to cause living beings to remove the obstruction of ignorance and the view of self and realize the inherent Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature. In brief, all Buddha-dharma is nothing but clarifying the mind and seeing the nature. And the mind and nature must be self-verified, because they are originally beyond what words can reach. Therefore it is said: the one who teaches the Dharma has no dharma to teach. Yet since living beings do not know it themselves, and one now wishes to teach them, one cannot but speak. And because obstructions are deep or shallow, one's speaking cannot but respond to their capacities. Therefore it is said: one speaks according to capacity. For if one speaks without matching capacity, they cannot understand, and what use is the speaking? Capacity has two senses: root capacity and timely capacity. Root capacity refers to the nature of their faculties, meaning that living beings' faculties differ one from another. Why do they differ? Because their obstructions are shallow or deep, thin or thick. Timely capacity refers to the time, that at one time he taught the Āgamas, at another the Vaipulya sutras, first the lesser then the greater, first the shallow then the deep, leading them on step by step and drawing them into the wonder, as in what is called the three periods and five periods. Therefore the dharma taught in forty-nine years is called the teaching of one age. “One age” means the Buddha's whole life. “Timely teaching” means giving teaching according to the time. Since he spoke according to capacity and gave teaching according to the time, the sutra teachings came to differ as half and full, provisional and real, gradual and sudden, partial and perfect. Therefore the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra likens the aspects of the teaching of one age to milk, or cream, or fresh butter, or clarified butter, and finally ghee. This is what is called the aspect of the teaching. For example, milk, cream, and the rest, though their names and marks differ, have one and the same wondrous use of nourishing the body and benefiting the person. So too with the sutra teachings. Though there are differences of name and mark such as half and full, partial and perfect, their guiding purpose is one: clarifying the mind and seeing the nature. This is the deep meaning of speaking in terms of aspect: it clarifies that one must not cling to the differing aspects, but should still converge and return to the non-differing nature. Yet since there are indeed various differing aspects, one should not cling to them, nor should one be muddled about them either. Therefore the ancients, with respect to the aspect of all sutra teachings, did not shrink from toil but discerned them and determined them. Though their views were shallow or deep and their accounts differed according to their standpoint, their intent was to benefit students, so that they might have the guiding principles and entries of the teaching of one age, its depths and shallows and its order, clear before their minds, and could advance in due order. Their painstaking care in benefiting later students is truly admirable. This is what is called judging the aspect of the teaching. Thus ends the explanation of the terms of judging the aspect of the teaching.
(G) Next, a general discussion of the aspects of teaching.

After the great Dharma came east, down to the end of the Jin, there were as many as eighteen houses that judged the teaching of one age, yet none of them was transmitted. In the writings of the ancients there are occasional citations of their accounts, a scale or a claw, but their whole was never seen. Judging from what is cited, they mostly discussed the broad outline only. From the Tang onward, what was commonly followed as relatively complete were the judgments of the two houses of Tiantai and Huayan. Tiantai judged the teaching of one age as the four kinds — Tripiṭaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect — which students called the four teachings. Huayan judged it as the five kinds — Lesser, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect — which students called the five teachings. What the Huayan school calls Lesser is what the Tiantai school calls Tripiṭaka, meaning the teaching of the lesser vehicle. That it is not called “lesser” is because the lesser vehicle, as to the three baskets of sutra, discipline, and treatise, though its meaning does not reach the fullness of the greater vehicle, yet possesses the three baskets completely. If it were called “lesser,” people might suspect its three baskets to be deficient and incomplete. Therefore it is not called lesser but Tripiṭaka. In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra the Buddha calls the lesser vehicle the teaching of half letters and the greater vehicle the teaching of full letters, because the lesser vehicle clarifies only the emptiness of the person, while the greater clarifies the emptiness of both person and dharmas, and so they are distinguished as half and full.

What the Tiantai school calls the Shared teaching, the Huayan school calls the Initial teaching. From here onward, all refer to the greater vehicle. It is called “shared” because its sutra meaning can reach down to the lesser vehicle and up to the Distinct and Perfect. In sum, the meaning it clarifies can be practiced in common by the three vehicles, and so it is named shared, which is to say ordinary or common. Whatever clarifies only the principle that person and dharmas are both empty belongs here. Contemplating emptiness is the initial gate of the greater vehicle, and so it is named the Initial teaching.

What is called the Distinct teaching: “distinct” means special. The Initial teaching only contemplates emptiness, the same as the two vehicles, and so it is called practiced in common by the three vehicles and named shared. Here, however, one does not only contemplate emptiness but also contemplates provisional existence, which the two vehicles do not practice in common; hence it is called distinct. The Huayan school names it the Final teaching, clarifying that one who practices the bodhisattva path, though at first contemplating emptiness, in the end does not abide in emptiness. In sum, the gates of practice of the greater vehicle from beginning to end are never apart from abiding in neither birth and death nor nirvāṇa. Furthermore, one first practices entering emptiness from the provisional, then practices emerging from emptiness into the provisional, each practiced separately, unlike the Perfect teaching's cultivating one and cultivating all. Thus it differs from both the Shared and the Perfect teachings. It is distinct below from the Shared and above from the Perfect, and so is called the Distinct teaching.

The Perfect teaching is what the Tiantai school calls the perfectly fused three truths of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, and what the Huayan school calls the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, the non-obstruction of phenomenon and phenomenon, one is all, and all is one. In sum, whatever sutra meaning embraces what are called the Lesser, Initial, Final, and Sudden, and what are called the Tripiṭaka, Shared, and Distinct, is the Perfect teaching.

The Huayan school inserts a Sudden teaching between the Final and the Perfect. Whatever sutra meaning clarifies that not a single thought arises, that one is a buddha in one's very substance, and that no stages are involved, belongs to it. The Tiantai school is not omitting this layer. One should know that the Tiantai judgment of teachings divides into the methods of conversion and the manners of conversion. The methods of conversion are the dharma-gates of instruction, namely the Tripiṭaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect; these refer to the purport of what was said in instructing. The manners of conversion are the forms of instruction, namely Sudden, Gradual, Secret, and Indeterminate; these refer to the appearances manifest in instructing. Speaking from the Buddha's side: to say it all at once is sudden. To speak in successive stages is gradual. To emit light to express the Dharma is secret. Not to speak definitively is indeterminate. Speaking from the hearers' side: to hear and immediately penetrate is sudden. Not to do so is gradual. To understand according to one's kind is indeterminate. Not to know one another is secret. Furthermore, when the sudden meaning is taught there is also the gradual meaning, and when the gradual meaning is taught there is also the sudden meaning. One person hears it as sudden, another takes it as gradual. What is originally sudden yields only gradual benefit. Though the Shared teaching is taught, the Distinct and Perfect are contained within it. And so even when the Tripiṭaka teaching is taught. Extending this to the rest, none is otherwise. All are what is called secret and indeterminate. In sum, the Tiantai school holds that among the four teachings of Tripiṭaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect there is none without sudden and gradual, and so it does not set up a separate gate. For it judges the teaching of one age by interweaving the methods of conversion and the manners of conversion with the common five periods and the distinct five periods. For this reason, in the fineness and perfect fusion of its judging of teachings, none surpasses Tiantai. Yet as to the principles and appearances of the teaching of one age, there is still something it does not fully gather in. One should know that this matter only a buddha with a buddha can exhaust. The patriarchs of the various schools had not reached the ground of buddhahood; though each had his own standpoint, how could they at once be equal to the Buddha? Later men need only choose the good and follow it. Thus ends the general discussion of the aspects of teaching, which is to say the first general discussion is finished. What follows is the direct judgment of this sutra's aspect of teaching.
(F) Next, the direct judgment.

The Tiantai school judges this sutra as Shared and Distinct together with Perfect; the Huayan school judges it as belonging to the Initial teaching, and also as reaching to the Perfect. Both inevitably cling to names and words, and do not fully accord with the sutra's purport. If one wishes now to determine what this sutra's aspect of teaching is, one cannot but first clarify this sutra's purport.

The Buddha spoke this sutra in order to open the inherent Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature in living beings and restore them to their original face. It is precisely the supreme and most profound dharma-treasure for continuing the Buddha-seed and transmitting the mind-seal. This one point alone is enough to prove that it is the teaching of utmost perfection and utmost suddenness. Being of utmost perfection and utmost suddenness, whatever is called Shared or Distinct, whatever is called Initial or Final, is all gathered in. How can one see that it has meanings such as Shared and Initial, and so cling to the words, inverting the account, and say that it merely includes the Perfect or reaches to the Perfect?

This sutra's principal purport lies solely in non-abiding. Non-abiding is not clinging. Not clinging is how the view of self is broken. Why? Because the view of self is deluded thought and attachment. The Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature is obstructed by the view of self. If one now wishes to reveal the nature, one must remove its obstruction. Therefore the one principal purport lies in non-abiding, by which the self is broken. Now wisdom and obstruction do not stand together. If one wishes to open and reveal the wisdom and awakened nature, one must indeed break the obstruction of the view of self. Yet opening and breaking are one continuous thread. To be able to break is to be able to open, and to be able to open is to be able to break. How, then, is this wisdom opened? It was said above: by arousing the one-substance great compassion. Compassion and wisdom both present is what is called the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi mind. This mind is one-substance compassion, and so one broadly cultivates giving and the six pāramitās in order to ferry all living beings into extinction and bring them to realize together the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature, without clinging to emptiness. To realize the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature is to enter nirvāṇa without residue. This mind is the wisdom of the principle-body. Therefore though one ferries living beings into nirvāṇa without residue, in truth no living being is ferried into extinction, and one does not cling to existence. Not clinging to existence is the markless. Not clinging to emptiness is the unmarked. Neither marked nor unmarked is precisely the true mark of the Tathāgata's wisdom and awakened nature. Therefore this sutra states this meaning as soon as it opens its mouth. And it plainly shows it, saying: one should not grasp dharmas, one should not grasp non-dharmas. This speaks of not clinging to the two extremes of emptiness and existence. With the least clinging, the view of self remains. With no clinging at all, the view of self is broken. For to ferry immeasurable, countless, boundless living beings into extinction, and yet in truth no living being is ferried into extinction — this is having no mark of self, person, and the rest. In truth no extinction, and so though one broadly practices the six pāramitās, one has no thought of dharmas — this is having no mark of dharmas. Though in truth no extinction, one does not cease ferrying — this is also having no mark of non-dharmas. Having no mark of self, person, and the rest is having no view of a person and a self. Dharmas and non-dharmas both absent is having no view of dharmas and a self. In other words: no mark of self, person, and the rest is what is called the emptiness of self. No mark of dharmas is what is called the emptiness of dharmas. And also no mark of non-dharmas is what is called the emptiness of emptiness, also called repeated emptiness. This speaks of being empty through and through. From this we see that this sutra's emptiness is to empty even emptiness, what is called being empty through and through. Being empty through and through is to conceal both extremes at once and illumine both extremes at once, what is called not abiding in emptiness or existence, perfect to the utmost. How can it be mentioned in the same breath as the Initial teaching that only contemplates emptiness?

And if one looks at what the sutra says at its opening, the meaning of the three emptinesses is present all at once. That is also cultivating one and cultivating all. How then could it be the Distinct teaching's meaning of first practicing entering emptiness from the provisional, then practicing emerging from emptiness into the provisional, separated and unfused? Moreover, being empty through and through and not abiding in either extreme is what is called being free of all marks. Only by being free of all marks does one arouse the bodhi mind. And being free of all marks, one is then called a buddha. For when all marks of emptiness and existence are gone, the mind is pure. When the mind is pure, reality is given rise to. The giving rise to reality is the breaking of ignorance and the view of self, and the appearing of the true-suchness dharma body. Therefore it is said: one is then called a buddha. Therefore it is said: if one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. Not only perfect to the utmost, but sudden to the utmost as well. Now being free of all marks is the arousing of the supreme bodhi mind, because it conceals and illumines at once and exactly accords with the middle way. And even the bodhi mind is not clung to, so that the middle too is not established. It goes so far as to say: all dharmas are Buddha-dharma. What are called all dharmas are likewise “is not” and yet “is called.” This is precisely what the Tiantai school calls: when one is empty, all is empty; when one is provisional, all is provisional; when one is middle, all is middle — the meaning of utmost perfect fusion. And it says: the Tathāgata means the suchness of all dharmas. It also says: this dharma is equal, with no high or low. This again is what the Huayan school clarifies: the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, the non-obstruction of phenomenon and phenomenon, one is all and all is one — the meaning of utmost perfect fusion. Everything said in the whole sutra is this meaning of utmost perfection and utmost suddenness. Yet it is judged as merely including the Perfect or reaching to the Perfect, as if the sutra's meaning were not wholly perfect. Why? In sum, the meaning of the whole sutra is nothing but the unfolding of the perfect and sudden non-abiding. But the first half mostly dislodges clinging with respect to the object. The object is all marks: the six dusts, the six faculties, the six consciousnesses, and even emptiness, existence, both, and neither are all included. Therefore the meaning of the first half may be summed up in a phrase: all is not, and no grasping at marks. Because there is no grasping, all is not. All is not and there is no grasping, and so ignorance and the view of self are broken, and the right wisdom of contemplation-prajñā shines out brightly. The latter half dislodges clinging with respect to the mind. The mind is the bodhi mind, the mind of the three periods, the mind that has something aroused and something attained, and all discriminating and clinging minds; all are included. Therefore the meaning of the latter half may be summed up in a phrase: all is, and no arising with respect to marks. Because there is no arising, all is. All is and there is no arising, and so ignorance and the view of self are utterly broken, and the principle-body of reality-prajñā appears in full clarity. Therefore in pointing out how it is to be expounded, it closes with two phrases: not grasping at marks, and thus without disturbance. It seems that because there is no grasping, one afterward is without disturbance; yet in fact one must be able to contemplate the undisturbed before one can be without grasping. This meaning was brought out in the first half. As it says: if the mind grasps at marks, then it clings to self, person, living being, and life span. For when the mind moves it grasps, and grasping it clings to marks. Therefore to be without clinging, one must not grasp. And to not grasp, the mind must be undisturbed. From this one sees that the meanings before and after are fundamentally one. It is only with respect to the outward text that there is a depth and an order, for the convenience of those who hear the Dharma with shallow or deep views.

It was said above that this sutra is the supreme dharma-treasure for continuing the Buddha-seed and transmitting the mind-seal. This one point alone is enough to prove that it is the teaching of utmost perfection and utmost suddenness. This is not an unfounded statement. This sutra says it repeatedly. For example: all buddhas, and the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi dharmas of all buddhas, all issue from this sutra. It also says: this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit. The Tathāgata speaks it for those who have aroused the greater vehicle, for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle. If someone can receive, hold, read, and recite it and widely explain it to others, the Tathāgata fully knows such a person and fully sees such a person, and all accomplish immeasurable, inexpressible, boundless, inconceivable merit. Such persons bear the Tathāgata's anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. It also says: former-world karmic deeds are thereby dissolved, and one shall attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. It also says: one should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rarest dharma. It also says: the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is also inconceivable.

Now to say that all buddhas issue from this sutra, and that one bears the Tathāgata's burden and shall attain bodhi — is this not continuing the Buddha-seed? To say that the Tathāgata speaks it for those who have aroused the greater and the supreme vehicle — is this not transmitting the mind-seal? To say that the sutra's meaning, karmic reward, merit, and accomplishment are all inconceivable — is this not the supreme dharma-treasure? Were it not the teaching of utmost perfection and utmost suddenness, how could it deserve such words? And it plainly says: all buddhas' anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi dharmas all issue from this sutra. Then all perfect and sudden sutra teachings are gathered in by this sutra. This sutra can gather in all sutra teachings, while all sutra teachings cannot gather in this sutra's teaching. Then as to utmost perfection and utmost suddenness, who could surpass this sutra? The Buddha's words are to be believed and must not be misrepresented. Therefore, reverently following the Buddha's intent, I judge this sutra to be the great teaching in which object and mind are both quiescent, concealing and illumining at once, wisdom penetrating the three emptinesses, and merit perfecting the ten thousand practices — utmost perfect and utmost sudden. All the various teachings of Tripiṭaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect, and of Lesser, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect, are gathered in at once. Its aspect is precisely like the supreme ghee, beyond the reach of milk, cream, fresh butter, and clarified butter.
Explaining the Title Concerning the Person
(B) Next, explaining the title concerning the person.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin

In the Jin period, within there were princes contending for power, and without the five barbarian peoples troubled China. Thus the various heroes partitioned the land and the whole country was thrown into disorder. Declining to the end of the Eastern Jin, the north had long since become a foreign domain, never enjoying a day of peace. There were in succession sixteen states, and the Yao Qin was one of the sixteen. Later Liu Yu destroyed the Jin and proclaimed the Song. The Qi, Liang, and Chen followed, and these were called the Southern Dynasties. In the north were the Yuan Wei, Zhou, and Qi, called the Northern Dynasties. Only afterward were they unified under the Sui, and then came to belong to the Tang, and the people were able to revive somewhat.

The Yao Qin established its capital at Chang'an, and its state was named Qin. To distinguish it from the former Qin of the Fu clan, it is called the Later Qin, and also the Yao Qin, because the ruler's surname was Yao. In the ninth year of the jianyuan era of Fu Jian of the former Qin (some say the thirteenth), a strange star appeared in the division of the western regions. The grand astrologer reported: a great and wise man of virtue will enter and assist China. Jian said: I have heard that in Kucha there is Kumārajīva, and in Xiangyang there is Dao'an — could it be these two? So he first sent courteous invitation to Master Dao'an. Then he dispatched the brave cavalry general Lü Guang with seventy thousand troops to attack Kucha, his intention being to obtain Kumārajīva. The Kucha army was defeated. Lü Guang obtained Kumārajīva, and on returning reached Xiliang. Hearing that Fu Jian had been murdered by Yao Chang, Lü Guang took possession of the Liang territory himself and called himself King of the Three Rivers, and detained Kumārajīva. When Yao Chang had murdered Fu Jian and proclaimed himself emperor, he repeatedly requested Master Kumārajīva, but Lü Guang would not consent. When Chang died, his son Yao Xing succeeded to the throne. He requested again, and again there was no consent. After Lü Guang's death, the succession passed to Lü Long. Yao Xing attacked him, and so welcomed Master Kumārajīva to Chang'an, honoring him as the state's teacher. He caused the monks Sengzhi, Sengrui, Sengzhao, and more than eight hundred others to gather under Master Kumārajīva's gate and greatly promote the work of translation. This was in the third year of the hongshi era of the Yao Qin. Our country's dharma destiny flourished from this. In Buddhism, nothing has been of greater consequence than this. During the Xiliang period, Lü Guang valued Kumārajīva only for his many stratagems, and did not at first promote the Way. Yao Chang likewise requested him only because he had heard the fame of his schemes. Yao Xing, however, was one who believed in the three gems.

Whoever can spread and promote the Buddha-dharma is called a dharma master. One who penetrates all three baskets of sutra, discipline, and treatise is called a Tripiṭaka master, a title even more solemn.

Kumārajīva in full Sanskrit is Kumārajīvapāda, and “jīva” is also written “Jīva.” His father was named Kumārāyaṇa, a man of India. His family had for generations been ministers of state; when he was about to succeed to the chancellorship he declined, withdrew, and left home, and journeyed east to Kucha. The king of Kucha, hearing that he had renounced honor, went out to the outskirts to welcome him and begged him to be the state's teacher. He forced him to take as wife his younger sister, named Jīva, and she bore Kumārajīva. Taking the names of both father and mother, he was named Kumārajīva. Such were the customs of India. His mother afterward bore another son, named Puṣyadeva. Then, longing for the Way and for austerities, she left home. Kumārajīva was then seven years old and left home with her. Kumārajīva means “youthful longevity,” meaning that in childhood he had the virtue of an elder. Daily he recited a thousand verses, in all thirty-two thousand words (thirty-eight words to each verse), and understood their meaning of himself. With his mother he went to Kashmir and took Bandhudatta as his teacher. He attacked and refuted the non-Buddhists and was able to subdue them. The king daily supplied him with the finest offerings. The monks of the monastery where he stayed appointed five senior monks and ten novices to sweep and sprinkle for him, as though they were his disciples. Such was the honor in which he was held. At twelve he returned with his mother to Kucha and traveled to Shale. The lesser vehicle teachings he penetrated completely. The king of Shale asked him to ascend the seat and teach. In his leisure he broadly read the non-Buddhist scriptures and treatises; the four Vedas, the five sciences, yin-yang, and astrology and calculation he exhausted entirely. He wondrously comprehended good and ill fortune, and his words matched like tally and seal. His nature was free and easy, and he did not sharpen himself in small restraints. Practitioners rather doubted him. Yet Kumārajīva was at ease in his own mind and never took it to heart. At that time there was Suryasoma, who devoted himself to spreading the greater vehicle. Kumārajīva also took him as his school and revered him. So he devoted himself wholly to the Vaipulya teachings. He recited the Madhyamaka and Śataśāstra and the Twelve Gates and others. The king of Kucha welcomed him back to the state to expound the sutras. At twenty he received the precepts. From Vimalākṣa he studied the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya. At that time his mother took leave of the king of Kucha and departed for India, having already reached the third fruit. As she was leaving she said to Kumārajīva: “The profound teachings of the Vaipulya should be greatly unfolded in China; to transmit them to the eastern land depends on your strength alone. But it will bring you no benefit yourself — what is to be done?” Kumārajīva said: “The way of the great being is to benefit the many and forget the body. If only the great transformation may spread and wash awake the deluded and ordinary, though I should lie in a furnace or cauldron, suffering without regret.” So he remained in Kucha. Later, in the old palace beside the monastery, he first obtained the Sutra of Emitting Light and read it. A demon came and obscured the text, so that he saw only blank tablets. Kumārajīva's mind grew firmer, the demon departed, and the characters appeared. Then he widely recited the greater vehicle sutras and treatises and penetrated their secret depths. The king of Kucha built him a golden lion throne and spread it with a brocade cushion of Greater Qin, and caused Kumārajīva to ascend it and teach. Bandhudatta came from no great distance. Kumārajīva was just then wishing to seek him out, and told him of the greater vehicle. So he debated with Datta over the meanings of the greater and lesser vehicles, back and forth with great effort. Only after more than a month did Datta believe and submit. He reversed his reverence and took him as teacher, saying: “I am the reverend's teacher in the lesser vehicle; the reverend is my teacher in the greater vehicle.” Whenever Kumārajīva went to various states to lecture, the kings would kneel long at the side of the seat and have Kumārajīva step over them to ascend the seat. Such was the esteem in which he was held. Since Kumārajīva's Way flowed through the western regions and his fame covered the eastern land, the former Qin's Fu Jian was determined to obtain him. Yet Lü Guang did not believe in the Buddha at all; though he obtained Master Kumārajīva, he subjected him to every kind of abuse, all of which the master endured. Later, because his words were never unfulfilled, Lü Guang began to regard him as extraordinary. Yao Xing had from youth revered the three gems, and having welcomed him to Chang'an, asked him to translate sutras in the Xiaoyao Garden. He also caused the famous monks Sengrui, Sengzhao, and others to consult and receive Kumārajīva's intent. From the time of Emperor Ming of the Han through the Wei and Jin, the sutras and treatises produced had often been clogged in wording and stilted in meaning. Kumārajīva read them and found much that did not correspond to the Sanskrit originals. So with Sengzhi, Sengqian, Daoheng, Daobiao, Sengrui, Sengzhao, and others, he first produced the Great Series. Yao Xing himself also held the sutra and collated it. Wherever the new text differed from the old, the meaning was perfectly coherent. The hearts of the multitude were satisfied and bowed, and none failed to rejoice and praise. Yao Xing also composed a Treatise on Penetrating the Three Ages to show the principle of cause and effect. Princes and dukes and all below praised the trend. He repeatedly asked Kumārajīva to lecture on the new sutras in the great monastery of Chang'an. Master Kumārajīva could speak Chinese. The sutras and treatises he translated amount to more than three hundred scrolls. The famous monk Daosheng penetrated the meaning of the scriptures subtly. He came specially through the pass to seek Master Kumārajīva's decision. The eminent monk Huiyuan of Mount Lu also often wrote to Kumārajīva to consult him on doubtful points in the sutras. Kumārajīva often told Sengrui that in the west they value literary form, and that in music and verse the melody is best when it fits the strings. Whenever one has an audience with a king, one must praise his virtue. In the ceremony of seeing the Buddha, chanting praise is held most noble. The verses in the sutras are all of this pattern. To change Sanskrit into Chinese loses its richness. Though one gets the general meaning, the literary form is quite sundered. It is like chewing food and giving it to someone: not only does it lose the flavor, it makes one vomit. Yao Xing worried that the seed of the Dharma would have no heir. He forced on him ten courtesans. From then on he did not dwell in the monks' quarters but set up a separate residence. Whenever he lectured, he often first said of himself: it is like a lotus growing from stinking mud. Pluck the lotus only; do not take the stinking mud. Some who saw the master in the company of women could not fathom his depths. The master took a handful of needles and said to them: “Can you swallow these needles? If you cannot, how can you study me?” From this one may know that Master Kumārajīva, in order to spread the great Dharma, had no choice but to provisionally show himself following conditions, while in truth he dwelt in mud without being defiled — how can one doubt him by outward traces? He died on the twentieth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of the hongshi era. As he was about to enter extinction he said to the assembly: “Unworthy as I am, I have presumptuously filled the role of translator. If what I have transmitted is without error, then after my body is burned let my tongue be undestroyed.” When it was cremated, it was indeed so.

The sutras and treatises he translated number ninety-eight in all, more than three hundred and ninety scrolls. Afterward a man came from India and said: of what Kumārajīva understood, not one part in ten was produced. This sutra is among what he translated. It was afterward translated again under the Yuan Wei, the Chen, and the Sui. In the Tang there were two more translations. In all there were six translations. Yet in ancient and modern times only the Qin translation has been honored in circulation. As to the facts of Master Kumārajīva's life, the ancients' writings often speak of them with considerable divergence. They do not altogether agree with what is recorded in the Biographies of Eminent Monks. Here I recount them briefly and do not venture on a detailed examination. In observing the matter of Master Kumārajīva's translation of sutras, there are two things we should attend to. (1) There are two great schools of sutra translation. One is the Kumārajīva school, which fuses the meaning of the whole sutra and conveys it in Chinese literary form. Therefore what it translates often does not entirely match the Sanskrit in phrases and sections. Yet no depth is left unrevealed and no subtlety unillumined. Easterners reading it find it especially suited to their capacities and easier to grasp. For it relies on the meaning and not on the words, which is what people today call free translation. The other is the Xuanzang school, which rigidly keeps the Sanskrit format and does not follow Chinese ways of expression. Easterners reading it find it very awkward, and the meaning is hard to grasp. This is probably what is today called literal translation. Now the spreading of the Buddha-dharma lies chiefly in making its meaning understood, not in studying Sanskrit. Then which school should be preferred for translated Buddhist sutras needs no argument. (2) Before Kumārajīva, because the translations were poor, not only were the profound and subtle meanings not conveyed, but even in the shallower matters many failed to state the teaching fully. Therefore few among the scholar-officials believed in Buddhism. After Master Kumārajīva's newly translated sutras and treatises appeared, and Elder Huiyuan at Mount Lu again strove to proclaim them, then men of letters and philosophers began gradually to understand Buddhist principle. The light of the Buddha-dharma then began like the newly risen sun, and by the Tang was like the sun at noon. Therefore after the great Dharma came east, it was only with Master Kumārajīva that it truly shone forth. Otherwise, though there were earlier the eminent monks Dao'an and later Huiyuan, they might not have been able to bring about the later flourishing. Why? Because the sutras and treatises they relied on were not sufficient in number or in clarity of meaning. Master Kumārajīva was a bodhisattva come again, and his disciples at the gate, such as Sengrui and Sengzhao, were profound in letters and principle, thoroughly versed in our country's old learning of Laozi, Zhuangzi, and the Six Classics. Teacher and disciples alike were no ordinary men. Therefore what they translated conveyed every principle and could sink deep into people's hearts. From the Song onward, the Buddha-dharma declined from its height, down to the extreme of today. And the country is in disorder and the people suffer, no different from the Jin period. At that time there was the spreading of Master Kumārajīva and his disciples, and the Buddha-dharma greatly flourished from it, people's hearts were improved by it, and the government gradually obtained peace by it. Then if one wishes the world to be at peace, one must first make people's hearts good. And if one wishes people's hearts to be good, one must first make the Buddha-dharma greatly flourish — this is clear. Look at the conditions of today: what are they like? Not only is the world in utter disorder; within Buddhism too there is utter disorder. There is no other reason: the true meaning of the Buddha-dharma is not understood. Therefore to make the Buddha-dharma greatly flourish, one must first understand the true meaning of the Buddha-dharma. And to understand the true meaning, one must first proclaim and spread the Diamond Prajñā, which continues the Buddha-seed. This depends on us all rising together to bear it.

Master Kumārajīva's translation of sutras began with the Great Series of Prajñā. Then if one wishes to bear the supreme bodhi dharma, one should begin with the Diamond Prajñā. Is this not luminously clear? With this vow, I dedicate it universally to all.
The essential purport of the Diamond Prajñā is summed up in eight characters: the principle reveals the three emptinesses, and contemplation fuses the two truths.

Begin with suffering, what is called the three sufferings and the eight sufferings. Suffering comes from karma, karma arises from delusion, namely the delusions of view and thought. Therefore they are explained in detail. And the root of delusion is the view of self. When the view of self is removed, the delusions do not arise. When they do not arise, there is no suffering of karmic bondage. This is what is called ending birth and death. The diamond is hard and sharp, a simile for prajñā's ability to cut off delusion. This sutra's guiding purpose lies solely in breaking the self. The coarse attachment to self is the four elements and five aggregates. The subtle is grasping at dharmas or at non-dharmas. Wherever there is grasping, the attachment to self is not yet exhausted. Therefore one must empty it layer upon layer: no mark of self, no mark of dharmas, and also no mark of non-dharmas. This is what is called the three emptinesses.

The character “dharma” has a broad meaning; every thing and every matter is included in it. The four elements and five aggregates are also among things. Therefore, speaking in terms of coarse and subtle, there is the mark of a person and a self and the mark of dharmas and a self. And speaking in terms of marks, they all belong to dharma. So the self of a person and the self of dharmas may be combined into one. All these things that have marks — the worldly eye regards none of them as unreal, and so they are called the conventional truth. “Truth” means truly real. Yet one may not know that all marks are delusive. It says that though they exist, they are unreal (existing yet not existing). To contemplate thus is called provisional contemplation. “No mark of non-dharmas” speaks of the nature of all dharmas. The mark is provisional, the nature is real; because the mark arises from conditions and the nature is unchanging, one knows it to be real, and so it is called the ultimate truth. To contemplate thus is called emptiness contemplation. Because the nature is originally without marks, it is called empty. Yet if one grasps at this mark of emptiness, that is one-sided emptiness, not the supreme-meaning emptiness of the greater vehicle (also called the emptiness of the highest meaning). Why? For example, empty space, though originally without marks, yet has the ten thousand marks ranged in it; indeed, only with the ten thousand marks ranged in it does it become empty space. One should know that the nature is the substance and the marks are the function. Where there is substance there must be function, and so where there is nature there must be appearing marks. But marks must not be clung to; clinging, one follows the marks and is blind to the nature, follows the function and is blind to the substance. Yet marks must not be annihilated either; annihilate the marks and, though one realizes the substance, what use is it, and indeed it does not become substance, since there is certainly no substance without marks. Therefore the meaning of the greater vehicle must be contemplated thus, and only then is it called emptiness contemplation (empty yet not empty). In this way the contemplation of the two truths is fused. Fused, it becomes the supreme truth of the middle-way contemplation. It is not that outside the two truths there is a separate supreme truth, nor that outside the provisional and emptiness contemplations there is a separate middle-way contemplation. What the sutra says in this way is called concealing expression, for it speaks by way of negation. Where the Lotus Sutra and others speak of the three truths, that is positive expression, for it speaks by way of revealing the two extremes of the nature's virtue as not clung to and both illumined. Concealing expression says that clinging to existence is wrong and clinging to emptiness is also wrong, and speaks of both extremes being dispelled, so that the two extremes are fused. Prajñā takes the dispelling of clinging as its guiding purpose, and so it speaks only of the two truths. One should know that ordinary beings' sickness lies in clinging everywhere, and so their deluded thoughts are many. One must first use the work of sweeping away, and only then can the nature's virtue be revealed. Therefore the World-Honored One first spoke prajñā and afterward spoke the Lotus. This meaning deserves the greatest attention. Again, the greater vehicle Buddha-dharma reaches from top to bottom. One must by no means exalt the sage's realm and think this is a matter of leaving the world, having nothing to do with worldly dharmas, for that betrays the Buddha's grace. One should know that if the three emptinesses and the two truths are not understood, one cannot even be a good person. Therefore I have expounded this principle fully. The above was spoken over three or so sessions.
