inline.s: (A) Next, a separate interpretation of the text's meaning, in three parts: (B) First, the introductory section. Next, the main teaching section. Third, the concluding section.
(A) Next, a separate interpretation of the text's meaning.

Meaning becomes manifest through words. And contemplation-prajñā and reality-prajñā both arise from textual prajñā. Then every word and every phrase of the sutra text must be examined and settled with certainty — this is clear. Now this sutra is widely read and recited, and so, in circulation from the Ming to the present, there are very many variant editions. Often they are corrupted or deficient in transmission, or meaning has been added or subtracted at will, each holding its own to be right, until one is almost at a loss what to follow. I, Xu, was born late; fortunately I have obtained the commentaries of the great masters of the Jin, Sui, and Tang, such as Sengzhao, Zhiyi, and Huijing, brought back from overseas. And Tang manuscript copies, as written by Liu Chengxuan and others and shut away in the Dunhuang caves, have also been discovered. Through them I have been able to collate them against one another and investigate, examining what is true and correcting what is false. This is truly a rare encounter, and also the responsibility of a later student. I have made a separate one-scroll Record of Textual Collation, appended after the sutra. As for differences of wording, where the presence or absence of a single character greatly affects the sutra's meaning, I now point them out one by one as they come, clarifying their purport. Which is right and which is wrong may then be plainly seen. Let the reader attend to it.

The sutra text is divided into three great sections. The first is called the introductory section. The second is called the main teaching section. The third is called the concluding section. No sutra is otherwise. This division began with Master Dao'an of the Eastern Jin, the teacher of Elder Huiyuan of Mount Lu, the first patriarch of the Pure Land school. When this account first arose, hearers doubted it. Afterward, when it was submitted to the Indian masters who came east, they learned that in the western land all sutras are divided in this way as well. Then they joyfully submitted, and it became a fixed rule. In this sutra, from “Thus have I heard” to “spread his seat and sat down” is the introductory section. From “At that time the elder Subhūti” to “this is called the mark of dharmas” is the main teaching section. From “Subhūti, if there is a person who fills immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds with the seven treasures and gives them away” to “believed, received, and practiced accordingly” is the concluding section.
(B) First, the introductory section, in two parts: (C) First, the prologue of attestation; next, the prologue of arising.
(C) First, the prologue of attestation.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

This prologue of attestation is also called the common prologue, because all sutras have it in common. It is also called the prologue after the sutra, because when the Buddha first taught a sutra there was originally no such prologue, and it was added only at the time of compilation. It is also called the prologue of the bequeathed teaching, because when the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, the venerable Ānanda, receiving the bequeathed command, was told that at the head of every sutra should be placed such words as “Thus have I heard; at one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a place, together with such-and-such an assembly, so many in number.” The purpose of placing “thus” and the rest is to prove that it was spoken by the Buddha, and so to arouse faith. Hence it is called the prologue of attestation.

The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra calls this section of text the six accomplishments. For whenever a sutra was compiled, six conditions had to be complete before it could be accomplished. What are the six conditions? First, “thus,” the accomplishment of faith. Second, “I heard,” the accomplishment of hearing. Third, “at one time,” the accomplishment of time. Fourth, “the Buddha,” the accomplishment of the master. Fifth, “in such-and-such a place,” the accomplishment of place. Sixth, “together with such-and-such an assembly of bhikṣus,” the accomplishment of the assembly. When the six conditions are complete, then the master who taught the Dharma, the time of teaching, the place of teaching, the assembly that heard the Dharma, and the compilers' responsible attestation that they themselves heard it — all that suffices to accomplish the faith of the assembly — each is present. Hence it is called the six accomplishments.

First, “thus”: “not different” is ru, “nothing amiss” is shi. When people believe, they say “so it is”; when they do not believe, they must say “it is not so.” Now the compilers, as soon as they opened their mouths, solemnly said “Thus,” thereby making clear that every word was as the Buddha spoke it, and that the wording and meaning were without error. Thus it suffices to be believed now and transmitted to later ages. Hence it is called the accomplishment of faith. The Avataṃsaka Sutra says: faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit, nourishing and fostering all good dharmas. Faith is the initial gate of entering the Way, and so it is placed first. Next, “I heard”: “I” is Ānanda's own designation. He deliberately says “I” as a word of responsibility, and also to make clear that he heard it with his own ears and did not transmit it at second hand. Above it continues “Thus,” and below it again details the assembly that heard it together, making clear also that it was not a private hearing. Thus “so it is, so it is,” and faith has its proof. Hence it is called the accomplishment of hearing.
